terms.advanced: The distinction carries real weight in a federal question: which list in the Ninth Schedule the subject falls under decides who could pass it at all, and a law outside the legislature's list is void under Art 4(1) whatever it says.

terms.gloss: Having a legal right to something, whether or not you ask for it.
terms.intermediate: Entitled means the right exists. It says nothing about whether the right has been claimed, or whether the court has any discretion about it.
terms.advanced: The word marks the divide between a remedy as of right and a discretionary one. A plaintiff is entitled to damages once breach and loss are proved; specific performance is never something anyone is entitled to.

terms.gloss: Property committed to someone for a purpose.
terms.intermediate: The element that makes s 405 apply: the accused received the property or dominion over it lawfully, on terms that constrained what he could do with it.
terms.advanced: Its opposite in a workplace context is mere custody, where the property remains in the employer's possession and the employee only handles it. The distinction decides whether taking it is theft or criminal breach of trust, and it turns on the scope of what was committed to the person rather than on physical proximity to the goods.

terms.gloss: Extension of time, under a construction contract.
terms.intermediate: More time to finish, granted under the contract's own machinery. Which events entitle the contractor to it, and what notice they must give, are set by the contract rather than by general law.
terms.advanced: The machinery matters as much as the entitlement: a claim good on its facts can fail on a notice provision. Read the clause before advising, because standard forms differ on both triggers and timing.

terms.gloss: Belonging to equity rather than to the common law.
terms.intermediate: An equitable right is one equity recognises even though the common law does not. An equitable remedy is one the court may give, but does not have to.
terms.advanced: The discretion is the point: damages come as of right once a breach is proved, while specific performance can be refused for delay, hardship or bad conduct even in a plain case.

terms.gloss: The body of rules developed to soften the common law's hard edges.
terms.intermediate: Equity began as the Chancellor's conscience and became a system of its own. It supplies remedies the common law will not give, such as specific performance and injunctions.
terms.advanced: Equity acts on the person, not the thing, and is discretionary — which is why clean hands, delay and hardship are arguments in equity and not at law. Section 3 of the Civil Law Act carries it into Malaysia.

terms.gloss: To prove to the court's satisfaction.
terms.intermediate: Establishing something is stronger than raising it. A defendant may only need to raise a defence; the prosecution must establish the offence.
terms.advanced: Watch which party must establish what. Under section 105 of the Evidence Act the accused must bring the case within an exception, while the prosecution retains the burden on the elements throughout.

terms.gloss: Everything a person owns — especially what they leave behind.
terms.intermediate: On death, the estate is collected, debts are paid, and what is left goes to those entitled. Someone must be appointed to do that.
terms.advanced: An executor's title comes from the will and is confirmed by probate; an administrator's comes only from the grant of letters of administration. The difference decides when they can lawfully deal with the assets.

terms.gloss: What a court is allowed to consider in deciding facts.
terms.intermediate: The material the court may look at — what witnesses say, and documents and things produced. Not everything true is evidence, because the Act decides what may be proved.
terms.advanced: The Malaysian Act inverts the English arrangement: Part I declares the categories of relevant fact, and nothing outside them may be proved. So the question is never whether something is relevant in the ordinary sense, but which section makes it relevant.

terms.gloss: A closed list of what may be proved and how.
terms.intermediate: Act 56. Evidence may be given of facts in issue and of such other facts as the Act declares relevant — and of no others.
terms.advanced: This is a different system from the English law of admissibility, where relevance is a general concept subject to exclusionary rules. Here the question is never simply 'is this relevant?' but 'which section makes this relevant?' If you cannot name one, the evidence does not go in, and an answer that argues fairness instead of citing a section has misunderstood the statute.

terms.gloss: The burden of putting enough evidence on a point to make it live.
terms.intermediate: Section 103 places the burden of proving any particular fact on the person who wishes the court to believe it. Unlike the legal burden, it shifts as the evidence goes in.
terms.advanced: It is the burden that is discharged by raising a point, not by persuading the court of it. An accused who raises a defence not covered by s 105 bears only this burden, and the prosecution must then disprove it to the criminal standard; where s 105 applies, the accused carries a legal burden instead.

terms.gloss: An application made without notice to the other side.
terms.intermediate: Used where giving notice would defeat the purpose — typically urgent injunctions. It carries a strict duty of full and frank disclosure.
terms.advanced: The applicant must disclose everything material, including matters that help the absent party; a breach of that duty is itself a ground for discharging the order, regardless of the merits. Ex parte relief is temporary by design, returnable on a date when the other side can be heard inter partes.
terms.source: Rules of Court 2012 O 29 and O 32

terms.gloss: A case the general rule deliberately leaves out.
terms.intermediate: An exception is part of the rule, not a defeat of it. Find the rule first, then ask whether the facts fall inside a recognised exception.
terms.advanced: Who proves an exception is a separate question from who proves the rule. Section 105 of the Evidence Act puts the burden of proving an exception on the accused, on the balance of probabilities.

terms.gloss: To use a power that has been given to you.
terms.intermediate: Public bodies exercise powers, and the exercise is what gets reviewed. Having a power is lawful; using it badly may not be.
terms.advanced: Discretion must be exercised, not surrendered: a body that applies a rigid policy without considering the case has fettered its discretion, which is a distinct ground of review.

terms.gloss: Whether something is there at all, as opposed to how far it goes.
terms.intermediate: Split every question in two: does the right exist, and what is its extent. Mixing them is how arguments go in circles.
terms.advanced: Section 101 of the Evidence Act frames the burden around the existence of facts. Existence questions are also where jurisdiction lives: a body cannot give itself power by finding that it has some.

terms.gloss: What a person has actually seen and done.
terms.intermediate: Experience does not lower a legal standard. A learner driver is judged by the standard of a competent one.
terms.advanced: It does matter in two places: where a statute makes it relevant, and where a professional holds themselves out as having a particular skill, which raises rather than lowers the standard.

terms.gloss: A numbered passage in a statute that clarifies the section above it.
terms.intermediate: Penal Code sections often carry Explanations and Illustrations. They are part of the Act and are read with the section, not as commentary.
terms.advanced: An Explanation cannot contradict the section it explains, but it can restrict or widen its apparent scope. Ignoring one is a standard way to misstate an offence.

terms.gloss: Expressing one thing implies the exclusion of others.
terms.intermediate: Where a provision names some cases, the argument runs that the ones it did not name were meant to be left out.
terms.advanced: The weakest of the linguistic canons and the most over-used. A drafter's silence is often just silence — a list may be illustrative, or the omission may be an oversight — so the canon carries weight only where the enumeration looks deliberate and complete. Courts frequently say so when rejecting it.

terms.gloss: Said in so many words, rather than implied.
terms.intermediate: An express term is written or spoken; an implied one is read in. Courts imply terms sparingly and never against an express one.
terms.advanced: Expressio unius rests on the same idea: what a statute mentions expressly suggests that what it leaves out was meant to be left out. It is a guide, not a rule.

terms.gloss: How far something reaches.
terms.intermediate: Legal answers are usually about extent, not existence. A duty exists — the fight is over how far it goes.
terms.advanced: Article 75 voids an inconsistent state law *to the extent of the inconsistency*, not entirely. Reading extent words carefully is what keeps a partial invalidity from becoming a total one.

terms.gloss: A fact that must be proved for the claim or charge to succeed.
terms.intermediate: The facts from which, either by themselves or with others, a right, liability or disability asserted in the proceeding necessarily follows.
terms.advanced: Facts in issue are fixed by the pleadings in a civil case and by the charge in a criminal one, which is why an imprecise pleading or charge causes evidential problems later. Relevant facts are a wider category: they are admissible because they bear on a fact in issue, not because they are one.

terms.gloss: Not doing something the law or an agreement required.
terms.intermediate: A failure is an omission with consequences. Failure to perform is breach; failure to appear can cost you the case.
terms.advanced: Liability for omissions is exceptional in tort and requires a duty to act — from a relationship, an undertaking, or control over the source of danger. The general rule is that there is no duty to rescue.

terms.gloss: Even-handed in procedure — not the same as producing a good outcome.
terms.intermediate: When lawyers say a hearing was unfair they usually mean the process was wrong: no notice, no chance to answer, a biased decider.
terms.advanced: Fairness in public law is the modern name for natural justice, and its content varies with context. A licensing renewal and a dismissal do not attract the same procedure.

terms.gloss: Blameworthiness — the reason the law attaches liability.
terms.intermediate: Most liability needs fault of some kind: intention, knowledge or carelessness. Some does not, and that is the exception worth noticing.
terms.advanced: Strict liability dispenses with fault as to one element, usually to make enforcement workable. It rarely dispenses with the act itself, so an involuntary act is still a defence.

terms.gloss: The supreme law of the Federation.
terms.intermediate: The document that creates the Federation, distributes legislative power, guarantees fundamental liberties and establishes the courts. Everything else in Malaysian law is subordinate to it.
terms.advanced: Its supremacy is stated in Art 4(1) and is the reason a legislative-competence argument exists at all: in a system of parliamentary sovereignty the question cannot arise. It is also amendable, generally by a two-thirds majority in each House, which is what makes the basic structure argument — whether some features are beyond even a valid amendment — worth having.

terms.gloss: The apex court of Malaysia.
terms.intermediate: The final appellate court, and the only court that may determine invalidity for want of legislative competence. Its decisions bind every court below.
terms.advanced: Access is not as of right in most civil matters: leave to appeal is required and is granted on limited statutory grounds, so a great many disputes end at the Court of Appeal. The Federal Court may depart from its own previous decisions, but does so sparingly and with reasons, which is why the sequence of authority in a moving area is worth stating rather than just the latest case.
terms.source: Courts of Judicature Act 1964; Federal Constitution Art 128

terms.gloss: An obligation of loyalty owed by someone trusted to act for another.
terms.intermediate: Its core is that the fiduciary must not profit from the position or allow a conflict between duty and interest without informed consent.
terms.advanced: Directors are the standard example, but the category extends to partners, agents, trustees and solicitors. The duty is one of loyalty rather than care, which is why a decision can be perfectly competent and still a breach — and why the business judgement rule protects the care duty only.
terms.source: Companies Act 2016 ss 213(1) and 218; general equitable principle

terms.gloss: Legal effect — or physical compulsion, depending on context.
terms.intermediate: A rule with the force of law can be enforced by a court. Force in the physical sense appears in assault, private defence and arrest.
terms.advanced: Subsidiary legislation has the force of law only within the enabling Act. Guidance and circulars usually have none, though they can generate a legitimate expectation.

terms.gloss: Something a reasonable person would have seen coming.
terms.intermediate: Foreseeability is judged objectively and in advance, not with hindsight. The question is what a reasonable person in the defendant's position would have anticipated.
terms.advanced: It appears twice in negligence and means different things: at duty it is about the class of person, at remoteness it is about the kind of damage. Wagon Mound made the second a separate hurdle.

terms.gloss: Making a false document to pass it off as genuine.
terms.intermediate: Forgery is about the document lying about who made it, not merely about the contents being untrue. A truthful statement on a document signed in someone else's name is still a forgery.
terms.advanced: In land, a forged instrument is one of the exceptions in section 340(2), and the fight is over whether the immediate transferee or a subsequent purchaser is protected by the proviso.
terms.source: Penal Code, ss 463-471; National Land Code, s 340

terms.gloss: A required form — writing, signature, registration, a witness.
terms.intermediate: Most contracts need no formality at all. Where a statute requires one, failing it can make the transaction unenforceable or void.
terms.advanced: Distinguish formalities that go to validity from those that go to proof. A dealing in land is ineffective without registration; a contract may be perfectly valid and merely harder to prove.

terms.gloss: The court or body with authority to hear the matter.
terms.intermediate: Choosing the wrong forum wastes the case. A tribunal, a syariah court and a civil court each have a defined reach.
terms.advanced: Article 121(1A) makes forum the first question in many family and religious disputes: if the matter is within syariah jurisdiction, the civil High Court has none, however strong the merits.

terms.gloss: A false suggestion, active concealment, or a promise made with no intention of performing.
terms.intermediate: Section 17's definition, covering acts done with intent to deceive or to induce a party to enter the contract. Mere silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak.
terms.advanced: The explanation to s 17 is the operative part in most problems: silence is fraud where the circumstances impose a duty to speak, or where silence is in itself equivalent to speech. Alleging fraud has procedural consequences too — it must be pleaded specifically and with particulars, and it is proved in civil proceedings on the balance of probabilities.
terms.source: Contracts Act 1950 s 17; Rules of Court 2012 O 18

terms.gloss: Consent not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake.
terms.intermediate: Section 14 defines it by what removes it, and ss 15 to 23 define each of the five. A contract requires free consent under s 10.
terms.advanced: The list is closed and each entry has a statutory definition much narrower than its everyday sense — coercion under s 15 means an act forbidden by the Penal Code or unlawful detention of property, not pressure at large. Consequences differ too: coercion, fraud and misrepresentation make the agreement voidable under s 19, while bilateral mistake as to an essential fact makes it void under s 21.

terms.gloss: A liberty the Constitution protects — and limits.
terms.intermediate: Constitutional freedoms are not absolute. Each comes with the grounds on which Parliament may restrict it, written into the same Article.
terms.advanced: Article 10 protects speech, assembly and association for citizens, subject to restrictions Parliament deems necessary or expedient on listed grounds. The fight is over how far *necessary or expedient* is reviewable at all.

terms.gloss: A contract becoming impossible or unlawful after it is made.
terms.intermediate: Section 57(2): a contract to do an act which after it is made becomes impossible, or unlawful for a reason the promisor could not prevent, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful.
terms.advanced: Malaysian law treats this as a statutory doctrine rather than the English implied-term or construction theories, and the consequence is automatic: the contract becomes void, and s 66 governs restoration. Mere hardship, increased expense or a bad bargain do not frustrate, and self-induced impossibility is not frustration at all.

terms.gloss: The spacing algorithm scheduling the cards in this app.
terms.intermediate: A model that estimates how durable each memory is and schedules the next review for the moment recall is predicted to fall to your chosen retention.
terms.advanced: It fits its estimates to the grades you give, which is why an honest Forgot is worth more than a flattering Hard: using Hard as a soft fail inflates every subsequent interval and quietly wrecks the schedule. Raising desired retention buys marginally better recall for a lot more reviews; the usual right response to poor recall is to re-atomise the cards instead.
terms.source: FSRS-6 via ts-fsrs, vendored in this app

terms.gloss: The rights in Part II of the Constitution.
terms.intermediate: Liberty of the person, equality, freedom of movement, speech, assembly and association, freedom of religion, rights in respect of education and property. They are enforceable against the State.
terms.advanced: Two structural points decide most problems. Some rights are held by citizens only — Art 10(1) speaks of citizens where Art 5 speaks of persons — so the claimant's status is a threshold question. And most rights are subject to restriction on stated grounds, so the argument is rarely whether the right exists and almost always whether the restriction falls within a permitted head.

terms.gloss: The case that set out the three grounds of judicial review.
terms.intermediate: Shorthand for the English decision that sorted judicial review into illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety. Malaysian courts use the same frame.
terms.advanced: The name is the initials of the body in the case, not a doctrine. Cite it for the classification of grounds; the Malaysian departure on how far a court may go comes from Rama Chandran, not from here.
terms.source: Standard classification of the grounds of review

terms.gloss: Chapter IV of the Penal Code, applying to every offence in it.
terms.intermediate: Sections 76 to 106: mistake of fact, judicial acts, accident, necessity, infancy, unsoundness of mind, intoxication, consent, and private defence.
terms.advanced: Section 6 makes every offence definition subject to them, though they are not repeated in the definition. The burden of bringing yourself within one lies on the accused under s 105 of the Evidence Act, on the balance of probabilities, and the court presumes their absence — that is a genuine legal burden and not merely an evidential one.
terms.source: Penal Code ss 6 and 76-106; Evidence Act 1950 s 105

terms.gloss: Real rather than pretended.
terms.intermediate: Genuine appears where the law tests sincerity: a genuine pre-estimate of loss, a genuine dispute, a genuine signature.
terms.advanced: A clause that is a genuine pre-estimate of loss is enforceable at common law. Section 75 of the Contracts Act sidesteps that inquiry and asks instead for reasonable compensation.

terms.gloss: Depart from the literal meaning where it produces an absurdity.
terms.intermediate: A traditional escape from a literal reading that would produce a result no legislature could have intended.
terms.advanced: Largely subsumed by the purposive direction, since an absurd result is unlikely to promote the Act's purpose. It survives as a way of describing the pressure point: the argument is really about how absurd a result has to be before the court concludes the words cannot mean what they appear to say.

terms.gloss: To control the answer — the rule that applies.
terms.intermediate: When a case says a section governs the question, it means look there first and stop looking elsewhere unless it sends you on.
terms.advanced: A governing provision displaces the common law only so far as it covers the ground. Section 3 of the Civil Law Act keeps English rules alive precisely where no local statute governs.

terms.gloss: The executive — federal or state — as a legal person.
terms.intermediate: The Government can sue and be sued, but on special terms. Claims against it follow a statutory procedure.
terms.advanced: The Government Proceedings Act 1956 sets the conditions, including notice requirements and limits on the remedies available. An injunction against the Government is a particularly restricted remedy.

terms.gloss: To give something formally — a right, an order or permission.
terms.intermediate: Courts grant orders; authorities grant licences; the state grants land. In each case the grantor has power to give and conditions to attach.
terms.advanced: In land, the state grant is the origin of title under the National Land Code, and the conditions in it — express and implied — bind every later proprietor.

terms.gloss: Exception 1 to s 300 — loss of self-control reducing murder.
terms.intermediate: Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, while deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation.
terms.advanced: Both adjectives do work: the provocation must be grave, judged with some regard to the accused's situation, and sudden, which is what a cooling-off period defeats. The Exception carries provisos of its own — it does not apply where the provocation was sought or voluntarily provoked, nor where it was given by something done in obedience to the law or in the lawful exercise of private defence.

terms.gloss: Serious, in the specific sense a statute defines.
terms.intermediate: Grievous hurt is not simply bad hurt. The Penal Code lists exactly what counts, and an injury outside the list is not grievous however painful.
terms.advanced: Section 320 gives eight kinds of grievous hurt, closing with hurt that endangers life or keeps the sufferer in severe bodily pain for twenty days. The list is exhaustive, and charging practice turns on it.

terms.gloss: A reason the law recognises for granting what you are asking for.
terms.intermediate: Grounds are not arguments in general — they are the recognised heads. Judicial review has three: illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety. Anything else has to be fitted into one of them.
terms.advanced: Naming the ground disciplines the pleading. A challenge that cannot be located in a ground is usually a complaint about the merits dressed as a complaint about legality.

terms.gloss: A promise to answer for another's default.
terms.intermediate: A promise that if someone else does not pay, you will. A bank asking a director to sign personally is asking for a guarantee.
terms.advanced: A guarantee is a secondary obligation, so it depends on the principal debt existing. It is the commonest hole in the protection of separate legal personality — not the shares and not the seat on the board, but a contract signed in the person's own name.

terms.gloss: Found by a court to have committed the offence.
terms.intermediate: Guilty is a verdict, not a description. Until a court says so, an accused is presumed innocent however strong the evidence looks.
terms.advanced: A plea of guilty must be unequivocal and made with an understanding of the charge, otherwise the conviction is liable to be set aside. That is a procedural safeguard, not a technicality.

terms.gloss: An order requiring a detainer to justify the detention.
terms.intermediate: The remedy for unlawful detention: the person holding the detainee must show lawful authority for doing so, or release them.
terms.advanced: It tests the legality of the detention, not its wisdom, and it is available even where a statute purports to make the detaining authority's decision final. Under detention legislation the practical scope of the inquiry has been narrowed by statute at various times, which is why the current provisions matter as much as the principle.
terms.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(2); Criminal Procedure Code Chapter XXXVI

terms.gloss: A settled way of doing something — occasionally evidence of what was done.
terms.intermediate: Evidence of habit can support an inference about a particular occasion, but it is weak on its own and easily over-read.
terms.advanced: Habit and character are different. Character evidence is tightly restricted by sections 52-55 of the Evidence Act; habit is relevant only where it bears on a fact in issue.

terms.gloss: Injury or loss of any kind, physical or financial.
terms.intermediate: A general word covering everything from a broken leg to a lost contract. Law usually needs it narrowed: which harm, to whom, caused by what.
terms.advanced: Not every harm is actionable. The question is whether the defendant owed a duty in respect of *this kind* of harm — which is why economic loss and psychiatric injury are treated separately from physical damage.

terms.gloss: The reporter's summary at the top of a reported case.
terms.intermediate: A headnote tells you what the case was about and what was held, in a few lines. It is written by the law reporter, not by the court.
terms.advanced: A headnote is not authority and has been wrong. Use it to decide whether to read the case, then cite the paragraph of the judgment that actually says what you claim.

terms.gloss: The occasion on which a court or body listens before deciding.
terms.intermediate: A hearing does not always mean an oral one. What fairness requires is a real opportunity to answer, which can sometimes be in writing.
terms.advanced: Audi alteram partem sets the floor. Its content is contextual: notice of the case, the substance of adverse material, and time to respond, scaled to what is at stake.

terms.gloss: What a court decided — the word that introduces the holding.
terms.intermediate: In a case note, *held* signals the court's actual decision on a point of law. It is the part later courts must follow.
terms.advanced: A headnote's *held* is the reporter's summary, not the court's words. Cite the paragraph of the judgment, because the headnote is not authority and has been wrong before.

terms.gloss: Unlimited original jurisdiction, and the first of the superior courts.
terms.intermediate: There are two of coordinate jurisdiction: the High Court in Malaya, and the High Court in Sabah and Sarawak. Neither binds the other.
terms.advanced: Coordinate means exactly that — a decision of one is persuasive in the other, and a High Court judge is not bound by another High Court judge, though departing from one is done with reasons because inconsistency at the same level is its own mischief. The High Court is also the forum for judicial review under Order 53 and for an order for sale of land held under Registry title.
aliases: High Court in Sabah and Sarawak

terms.gloss: House of Lords — the former highest court in the United Kingdom.
terms.intermediate: The UK's top court until 2009, when the UK Supreme Court replaced it. Its decisions appear in English citations as (HL).
terms.advanced: Salomon, the case that settled separate corporate personality, is a House of Lords decision from 1897 that Malaysian courts apply. Age alone is not a reason to distrust a decision; some old ones hold up better than recent ones.

terms.gloss: The same in every respect that matters.
terms.intermediate: Cases are never identical in fact. The question is whether they are alike in the respects the rule makes relevant.
terms.advanced: That is the whole of distinguishing. A difference that did not matter to the earlier ratio is not a ground for departing from it, however striking it looks.

terms.gloss: A worked example printed inside a statute.
terms.intermediate: The Contracts Act and Penal Code contain lettered illustrations. They show how the section is meant to work on facts.
terms.advanced: Illustrations are part of the Act and are strong guides to construction, though they cannot override the section's clear words where the two genuinely conflict.

terms.gloss: Done for the wrong reason, or in the wrong way.
terms.intermediate: Improper purpose is a ground of review: the power was used for something it was not given for. The decision can be perfectly reasonable and still unlawful.
terms.advanced: Improper purpose overlaps with irrelevant considerations and bad faith but is distinct. Bad faith requires dishonesty; improper purpose does not.

terms.gloss: In a definition, to add to the ordinary meaning rather than replace it.
terms.intermediate: *Includes* extends: the word keeps its normal sense and gains what follows. *Means* replaces it entirely.
terms.advanced: Reading *includes* as exhaustive is one of the most common interpretation errors, and it narrows statutes that Parliament wrote to be wide.

terms.gloss: Unable to stand together — one contradicts the other.
terms.intermediate: Inconsistency is a legal test, not just an observation. A state law inconsistent with a federal law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.
terms.advanced: Article 75 requires a real conflict, not merely overlapping subject matter. Two laws that can both be obeyed are not inconsistent, however untidy the overlap.

terms.gloss: A registered title that cannot be set aside.
terms.intermediate: Section 340(1): the title or interest of a registered proprietor is indefeasible, subject to the exceptions in s 340(2) — fraud or misrepresentation, forgery or an insufficient or void instrument, and unlawful acquisition.
terms.advanced: Malaysian law applies deferred, not immediate, indefeasibility: a proprietor registered through a forged or void instrument takes a defeasible title, while a subsequent purchaser in good faith and for value takes a good one. Adorna Properties held the opposite and stood for nine years before Tan Ying Hong departed from it, so anything written on the topic before 2010 must be dated before it is trusted.
terms.source: National Land Code s 340; Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 (FC); Adorna Properties Sdn Bhd v Boonsom Boonyanit [2001] 1 MLJ 241 (FC)

terms.gloss: A promise to make good another's loss.
terms.intermediate: An undertaking to cover someone else's loss if it happens. It stands on its own, without needing anybody else to default first.
terms.advanced: That independence is what separates it from a guarantee: an indemnity is a primary obligation, so it survives circumstances that would discharge a surety, and it is not defeated merely because the principal obligation turns out to be unenforceable.

terms.gloss: A conclusion drawn from a proved fact rather than stated directly.
terms.intermediate: Something the court works out from other facts, instead of being told outright. Nobody saw the theft, but the goods were in his room the next morning.
terms.advanced: An inference must be the reasonable conclusion from proved facts, not a guess dressed as one. Where an inference is permissive the court may draw it and is never bound to, which is the difference between s 114's illustrations and a presumption the court must make.

terms.gloss: Facts communicated — and, in procedure, the report that starts a case.
terms.intermediate: A first information report starts a police investigation. Information in the wider sense is what evidence conveys.
terms.advanced: Section 27 of the Evidence Act makes so much of information received from an accused admissible as leads to a discovery of fact, which is a narrow and heavily litigated exception to the rules on confessions.

terms.gloss: Harm to a person's body, mind, reputation or legal rights.
terms.intermediate: Personal injury is the everyday sense. But law also speaks of injury to a right — a wrong done to your legal position, even without a bruise.
terms.advanced: Injuria sine damno (a wrong without loss) is actionable in torts that protect a right as such, like trespass. Damnum sine injuria (loss without a wrong) is not actionable at all.

terms.gloss: What a person meant to do or bring about.
terms.intermediate: Intention is a state of mind, proved by conduct rather than confession. Courts infer it from what was done and said.
terms.advanced: Distinguish intention in crime, where it grades the offence, from intention in contract, where it is objective — what a reasonable person would take the words to mean, not what the speaker privately meant.

terms.gloss: Mixing topics in a session rather than blocking them.
terms.intermediate: Studying contract and criminal law in the same sitting rather than one after the other. It feels worse and produces better discrimination between them.
terms.advanced: Blocked practice lets you apply the same rule repeatedly without deciding which rule applies — which is the very skill an issue-spotting problem tests. Interleaving forces the choice each time, and the cost is that performance during practice drops, which learners routinely misread as the method not working.
terms.source: Make It Stick; the interleaving literature

terms.gloss: An order holding the position until trial.
terms.intermediate: The applicant must show a serious question to be tried, that damages would not be an adequate remedy, and that the balance of convenience favours the injunction. An undertaking in damages is ordinarily required.
terms.advanced: The court does not try the merits, which is why an argument that the applicant will probably win is beside the point. A mandatory injunction — requiring something to be done rather than restrained — attracts a higher threshold, and the Malaysian gloss on American Cyanamid should be cited from a Malaysian decision rather than an English one.
terms.source: Rules of Court 2012 O 29; American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396 as applied in Malaysia

terms.gloss: Settling what a provision means.
terms.intermediate: Deciding what the words of an Act actually require. You start with the words themselves, then their place in the Act, then what the Act was for.
terms.advanced: Section 17A requires a purposive approach, so a reading that promotes the underlying object is preferred to one that does not. The internal aids — long title, marginal notes, provisos, definition sections — come before external material.

terms.gloss: The police stage of a criminal case, before anyone is charged.
terms.intermediate: Investigation gathers evidence: statements, searches, seizures. Charging comes afterwards, and the decision to charge is not the police's alone.
terms.advanced: Chapter XIII of the Criminal Procedure Code governs police investigation, and statements recorded under section 112 are subject to strict limits on later use at trial.

terms.gloss: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion — a structure for making reasoning visible.
terms.intermediate: A way of ordering an answer so that the rule is stated before it is used and the application is separated from the recitation. It is scaffolding, not a form to be filled.
terms.advanced: Its value is that it forces the step people skip when unsure: stating the governing rule with its source before reasoning from it. Its characteristic failure is a long Rule section and a thin Application — an answer that proves recall and not reasoning, which is why rubric bands weight application most heavily.

terms.gloss: The officer who decides the case and gives reasons for it.
terms.intermediate: A judge finds the facts (unless a jury does), applies the law, and writes the judgment. What binds later courts is the reasoning, not the result.
terms.advanced: Judicial power is vested by Article 121. A judge's own view of good policy is not a source of law, which is the whole point of the distinction between ratio and obiter.

terms.gloss: The power to decide disputes according to law, and whether the Constitution still vests it.
terms.intermediate: Before 1988 Article 121(1) vested the judicial power of the Federation in the High Courts. The amendment replaced that with jurisdiction 'conferred by or under federal law'.
terms.advanced: On one reading the courts' jurisdiction became entirely a creature of statute; on another, judicial power is inherent in a constitution that separates the branches and cannot be removed by rewriting the sentence describing it. Malaysian courts have taken both views at different times, and this is the most unsettled area in the constitutional module — do not state either position as settled without checking the most recent Federal Court authority.

terms.gloss: The court reviewing how a public decision was made, not whether it was right.
terms.intermediate: Brought under Order 53 with leave. The grounds are illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety, with proportionality argued as a fourth.
terms.advanced: Review goes to the decision-making process, which is why it is not an appeal. Malaysian law has gone further than English law in places: R Rama Chandran allows a court in an appropriate case to examine substance and to substitute its own decision rather than remitting — though later authority has been careful about the limits, and the case should be cited for what it decided rather than for the proposition that review is now an appeal.
terms.source: Rules of Court 2012 O 53; R Rama Chandran v Industrial Court of Malaysia [1997] 1 MLJ 145 (FC)

terms.gloss: The range of people and matters a court may decide.
terms.intermediate: Whether this court is allowed to hear this case at all. It has two halves: the kind of matter, and the people or the place involved. A court without jurisdiction cannot cure that by deciding the case well.
terms.advanced: Every Malaysian court below the Constitution's own heads takes its jurisdiction from statute, so the question is always which provision confers it. Keep three things apart: whether a court has jurisdiction, whether it should exercise one it has, and whether the decision it reached was right. Only the first is jurisdiction.
terms.source: Courts of Judicature Act 1964; Subordinate Courts Act 1948

terms.gloss: Suitable for a court to decide.
terms.intermediate: Some questions have no legal standard to decide them by — whether a policy was wise, for example. Those are said not to be justiciable.
terms.advanced: Non-justiciability is about the nature of the question, not the identity of the decision-maker. A minister's decision on legality is reviewable even where the same minister's decision on priorities is not.

terms.gloss: To cause the death of another person.
terms.intermediate: Killing is not automatically murder. The same act can be murder, culpable homicide, or no offence at all, depending on state of mind and defences.
terms.advanced: Section 299 defines culpable homicide; section 300 lifts it to murder in four situations, and the exceptions to section 300 bring it back down. Read the ladder in that order.

terms.gloss: Actually knowing something — a state of mind the law often requires.
terms.intermediate: Many offences and liabilities need knowledge, not just carelessness. Proving it usually means proving what the person must have realised.
terms.advanced: Knowledge sits between intention and negligence on the fault ladder. Section 26 of the Penal Code defines *reason to believe*, which is lower than knowledge and higher than mere suspicion.

terms.gloss: The person who grants a lease or tenancy of land.
terms.intermediate: The landlord keeps ownership and gives away possession for a period. What is left is called the reversion — the right to have the land back.
terms.advanced: Distinguish a landlord's contractual rights from proprietary ones. A registered lease binds a purchaser of the reversion; a mere agreement to lease may not.

terms.gloss: Permitted by law.
terms.intermediate: Lawful means the law allows it. It does not mean the law requires it, and it does not mean it is a good idea.
terms.advanced: Watch the load the word carries in a defence. Lawful authority, lawful excuse and lawful justification are separate doorways, and pleading the wrong one loses a winnable point.

terms.gloss: Glanville Williams, Learning the Law — the method book this course leans on.
terms.intermediate: An introduction to reading statutes and cases, solving problem questions and studying law. Edited by A. T. H. Smith, 18th edition, Sweet & Maxwell.
terms.advanced: Its framing is the English legal system, so take the method and not the substantive law. How to read a section, brief a case and structure an answer transfers to Malaysia unchanged; what the law says does not.
terms.source: Glanville Williams, Learning the Law, 18th ed (Sweet & Maxwell), ed A. T. H. Smith

terms.gloss: A registered interest giving the right to occupy land for a term.
terms.intermediate: A right to occupy someone else's land for a fixed period. A registered lease is an interest in the land itself, which is more than a tenancy agreement between two people.
terms.advanced: Registration is what makes the difference: a registered lease binds a later proprietor, while an unregistered arrangement generally binds only the parties to it. The register is where you find out which one you are dealing with.

terms.gloss: The risk of losing if the fact is not proved. It does not shift.
terms.intermediate: Section 101: whoever asserts facts on which a right or liability depends must prove them. Section 102 identifies who carries it by asking who would fail if no evidence were given.
terms.advanced: Its counterpart, the evidential burden under s 103, is the burden of adducing evidence on a particular fact, and that does move as the case develops. Saying 'the burden shifted' without saying which one is the standard imprecision in this area, and it matters most in criminal cases, where the legal burden stays on the prosecution except where a statute places one on the accused.

terms.gloss: Whether the legislature had power to pass the law at all.
terms.intermediate: Parliament may legislate on the Federal and Concurrent Lists; a State Legislature on the State and Concurrent Lists. A law outside the allotted field is invalid however sensible it is.
terms.advanced: Competence is the prior question in any constitutional problem, and it is often decisive without reaching rights at all: a restriction contained in an ultra vires statute fails before Article 10 is ever considered. The Federal Court has exclusive jurisdiction under Art 128 to determine invalidity on this ground, so getting the forum right is part of the answer.
terms.source: Federal Constitution Arts 74, 4(1) and 128; Ninth Schedule

terms.gloss: An expectation founded on a clear representation or a settled practice.
terms.intermediate: Most secure in its procedural form: that a person will be consulted or heard before a change. The substantive form — that the benefit itself will be conferred — is more contested.
terms.advanced: An expectation cannot be legitimate if the representation was outside the decision-maker's power, because a public body cannot bind itself to act unlawfully. The reception of substantive legitimate expectation in Malaysia should be checked against current authority rather than asserted, and a settled practice described in a published leaflet is exactly the kind of material that founds the procedural form.
terms.source: Standard administrative law; the Malaysian authorities on legitimate expectation

terms.gloss: What an agreed-damages clause is allowed to protect.
terms.intermediate: The innocent party's genuine commercial interest in performance, beyond simply being compensated in money. The test asks whether the stipulated sum is out of all proportion to it.
terms.advanced: It comes into Malaysian law through Cubic Electronics, which drew on Cavendish v Makdessi, and it shifted the focus away from the old genuine-pre-estimate question. Timely completion of a revenue-producing asset is the standard example of such an interest; deterrence for its own sake, unmoored from any interest in performance, is not.
terms.source: Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd [2019] 2 MLJ 806 (FC)

terms.gloss: Being legally answerable for something.
terms.intermediate: Being on the hook: the law says you must pay, compensate or answer for what happened. Establishing liability is a separate question from how much is owed.
terms.advanced: Keep liability and quantum apart in an answer. A party may be liable and owe very little, or be plainly at fault and owe nothing because the damage was too remote. Merging the two is a standard way to lose marks in tort.

terms.gloss: Defamation in permanent form.
terms.intermediate: Written, printed or otherwise recorded defamation. It is actionable without proof of special damage.
terms.advanced: How internet publication is classified has made the permanent-or-transient line harder to apply than it sounds, and the current Malaysian position should be checked rather than assumed. Each republication is generally a fresh publication, which is what makes online material a continuing exposure rather than a single event.

terms.gloss: Permission to do something that would otherwise be wrong.
terms.intermediate: A licence makes lawful what would be a trespass or an offence. It gives permission, not ownership — a licensee on land has no interest in it.
terms.advanced: The line between a licence and a lease is exclusive possession, not what the parties called the document. Getting it wrong changes whether the occupier has any right the courts will protect against a new owner.

terms.gloss: The way a deposited title document is protected as security.
terms.intermediate: Where the issue document of title is deposited with an intention to create security, the lien is protected — and becomes enforceable — by entering a lien-holder's caveat.
terms.advanced: Facts that mention a deposited title document are almost always testing this rather than a private caveat, and recognising the cue is faster than reasoning from first principles. The lien is an informal security that the Code accommodates rather than creates, which is why the caveat does more work here than it does elsewhere.
terms.source: National Land Code, the caveat provisions

terms.gloss: Probable — the word most legal standards are built from.
terms.intermediate: *Likely* usually means more probable than not. That is the civil standard, and it is lower than the criminal one.
terms.advanced: Section 74 of the Contracts Act uses knowledge of what was *likely* to result to fix the outer limit of recoverable loss. Likelihood is judged at the time of contracting, not at breach.

terms.gloss: One branch of a test that has several parts.
terms.intermediate: When a rule has three requirements, lawyers call each one a limb. Saying which limb fails is more useful than saying the test is not met.
terms.advanced: Limbs can be cumulative or alternative, and the difference decides the case. Caparo's three are cumulative; the grounds of judicial review are alternatives.

terms.gloss: The period within which an action must be brought.
terms.intermediate: Generally six years for contract and tort under the Limitation Act 1953, and twelve for actions to recover land, running from when the cause of action accrued.
terms.advanced: Accrual is not the same as the wrongful act: in contract it runs from breach, in negligence generally from when damage occurs, which may be much later. Limitation is a defence that must be pleaded, and other statutes contain their own periods — public authorities and certain claims are subject to shorter ones — so the general period must be checked against the particular claim.

terms.gloss: A sum the contract fixes as payable on breach.
terms.intermediate: An agreed figure intended to save the trouble of proving loss. In Malaysia its effect is governed by s 75 rather than by the English penalty rule.
terms.advanced: The parties' own description of the sum as a genuine pre-estimate is evidence and not conclusive; a label cannot convert a disproportionate sum into a proportionate one. Under the Cubic Electronics approach the questions are whether the clause protects a legitimate interest and whether the sum is out of all proportion to it, and causation still has to be established — a claimant cannot recover for a loss the breach did not cause.

terms.gloss: Give the words their ordinary meaning.
terms.intermediate: The starting point of any construction: read what the provision says. Purpose does not licence ignoring the text.
terms.advanced: The literal approach is often presented as the opposite of the purposive one, which is misleading. They answer different questions: the literal reading establishes the range of meanings the words can bear, and the purposive direction chooses among them. A provision whose words admit only one meaning is not made ambiguous by the fact that the meaning produces an inconvenient result.

terms.gloss: Money lent, to be repaid on agreed terms.
terms.intermediate: A loan creates a debt from the moment it is drawn down. Security is separate: it is what the lender can seize if the debt is not paid.
terms.advanced: A loan agreement and the charge securing it are distinct contracts with distinct remedies. A defect in the charge does not extinguish the debt, and a paid debt does not automatically clear the register.

terms.gloss: Standing to bring the proceedings.
terms.intermediate: Whether this applicant is entitled to ask the court to decide this question. In judicial review the Malaysian test is whether the applicant is adversely affected by the decision.
terms.advanced: It is a threshold, not a merits question, though the two blur in practice because a person plainly affected usually has a real complaint. The Malaysian formulation is narrower than the English one, which is why an answer that imports 'sufficient interest' has stated the wrong test.
terms.source: Rules of Court 2012 O 53; the Malaysian authorities on standing

terms.gloss: The opening words describing what an Act is for.
terms.intermediate: 'An Act to provide for…' — admissible evidence of the Act's purpose, and part of the enacted text.
terms.advanced: Unlike a marginal note, the long title is enacted and may be used to resolve an ambiguity, though it cannot cut down clear words in a section. It is the first place to look when an argument needs the Act's object, and it is routinely overlooked.

terms.gloss: The base of the ordinary hierarchy.
terms.intermediate: Handles lower-value civil claims and less serious criminal matters, with sentencing powers capped by statute.
terms.advanced: It is also the court that authorises remand under s 117 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which is a function quite separate from trying cases and is where most people first encounter it. Its civil and sentencing limits are statutory and are raised from time to time.
terms.source: Subordinate Courts Act 1948; Criminal Procedure Code s 117

terms.gloss: The judges who agreed on the result — whose reasoning counts.
terms.intermediate: In an appellate court the majority decides. A dissent is worth reading but binds nobody.
terms.advanced: Where the majority agree on the result for different reasons, finding the ratio is harder: look for the narrowest reasoning that commands majority support.

terms.gloss: An improper motive that destroys a defence.
terms.intermediate: In defamation it defeats qualified privilege and fair comment. It is not an element of the tort, and proving hostility does not by itself establish liability.
terms.advanced: Malice here means using the occasion for a purpose other than the one for which it is protected, or making the statement without honest belief in its truth — spite is evidence of it rather than the definition. Because it is directed at defences, the sequence in an answer matters: elements, then defence, then malice.

terms.gloss: An order compelling performance of a public duty.
terms.intermediate: Requires a public body to do what the law obliges it to do. It does not dictate how a discretion is exercised, only that it be exercised.
terms.advanced: The distinction matters: a court will order an authority to decide, and will not usually order it to decide in the applicant's favour. Where the duty is owed to the public generally rather than to the applicant, standing becomes the difficulty.

terms.gloss: A requirement that must be met, as against one that may be.
terms.intermediate: Something the law says must happen. Shall is usually mandatory; may usually leaves a choice. The two words decide cases.
terms.advanced: Courts read shall and may in context rather than mechanically, and a may has been read as a duty where the power exists for somebody else's benefit. Where a requirement is mandatory, the further question is what follows from breach — invalidity, or a defect that can be cured.

terms.gloss: The heading printed beside a section. Not enacted text.
terms.intermediate: A drafting convenience indicating what a section is about. It orients a reader but cannot control the meaning of a clear provision.
terms.advanced: Marginal notes and headings are inserted for arrangement and are not voted on, which is the reason for their limited weight. They may be used as an indication of the drafter's intention where the words are genuinely ambiguous, and citing one as though it were operative is a visible error.

terms.gloss: A legally recognised union, with consequences the parties cannot fully choose.
terms.intermediate: Marriage changes legal status, not just living arrangements. It affects property, maintenance, children and inheritance.
terms.advanced: Malaysia runs two systems side by side: the Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976 for non-Muslims, and syariah law administered by state authorities for Muslims. Jurisdiction is decided first, and Article 121(1A) keeps the civil courts out of matters within syariah jurisdiction.
terms.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976; Article 121(1A)

terms.gloss: A fact the decision turned on — one whose change might change the result.
terms.intermediate: The facts that carried legal weight, as opposed to the ones that merely tell the story. Identifying them is most of the work of reading a case.
terms.advanced: Materiality is a counterfactual test, and it is contestable: two lawyers can read the same judgment and disagree about which facts were doing the work, which is exactly what an argument about the scope of a precedent consists of. In pleading, the phrase means something adjacent but distinct — the facts that must be pleaded to disclose the cause of action, as opposed to the evidence that will prove them.
terms.source: Standard common law method; Rules of Court 2012 O 18 for the pleading sense

terms.gloss: Testing the prosecution evidence properly at the halfway stage.
terms.intermediate: The requirement that a court deciding whether a prima facie case exists evaluate the credibility of the prosecution evidence, not merely ask whether any evidence was led.
terms.advanced: The phrase comes from the judicial discussion around the amendments to s 180 and its predecessor, and the standard has moved more than once — which is why the current formulation should be taken from a recent decision rather than a summary. Its practical effect is that a submission of no case is a real argument about the quality of the evidence.
terms.source: Criminal Procedure Code s 180 and the case law upon it

terms.gloss: What words in a statute or contract are taken to signify.
terms.intermediate: Meaning is decided by the court, not by what the writer says they meant. The question is what the words convey to a reasonable reader in context.
terms.advanced: Ordinary meaning, technical meaning and defined meaning are three different things, and a definition section beats all the others within its Act.

terms.gloss: A shareholder, seen from the company's side.
terms.intermediate: The register of members is the company's own list of owners. Rights against the company — to vote, to petition, to sue — belong to members.
terms.advanced: Membership, not shareholding in fact, gives standing under sections 346 and 347. Someone holding shares beneficially through a nominee is not on the register and must act through the nominee.

terms.gloss: What you can retrieve later — the point of studying at all.
terms.intermediate: Recognising a rule when you see it is not the same as being able to produce it. Only the second survives an exam or a client meeting.
terms.advanced: Retrieval practice and spacing beat rereading by a wide margin in the evidence, which is why this app tests rather than displays. Difficulty during study is a feature, not a fault.

terms.gloss: The guilty mind — the mental element of an offence.
terms.intermediate: Intention, knowledge, recklessness or negligence, as the particular offence requires. It is presumed to be required unless a statute displaces it.
terms.advanced: In a codified system the phrase is a category rather than a test: the Penal Code specifies the fault element for each offence, and 'intending to cause death' or 'knowing it to be likely' is what has to be proved, not mens rea in the abstract. The presumption that a criminal offence requires a mental element is displaceable expressly or by necessary implication, and strict liability is not lightly inferred.
terms.source: Penal Code; standard presumption of construction

terms.gloss: To do with the mind — the fault side of an offence.
terms.intermediate: Every offence has a physical part and usually a mental part. Proving the act without the required state of mind proves nothing.
terms.advanced: Mental element and motive are different. Motive is why someone acted and is never an element; the mental element is what they intended or knew, and it always is where the section says so.

terms.gloss: 31 August 1957 — the date the supremacy clause runs from.
terms.intermediate: Independence day for the Federation of Malaya, and the reference point in Article 4(1) for which laws are tested against the Constitution.
terms.advanced: The date matters technically as well as symbolically: Art 4(1) speaks of law passed after Merdeka Day, and pre-Merdeka law is dealt with separately, with Art 162 providing for its continuation subject to modification to bring it into accord with the Constitution. Malaysia itself was formed later, in 1963, which is why the reception dates in the Civil Law Act 1956 differ between the peninsula, Sabah and Sarawak.

terms.gloss: Whether a decision was right — as opposed to whether it was lawfully made.
terms.intermediate: Judicial review is not an appeal. The court asks whether the decision-maker stayed within the law, not whether it would have decided the same way.
terms.advanced: Wednesbury is the boundary marker: a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could reach it becomes a legality question. Below that line the merits belong to the decision-maker.

terms.gloss: A repeatable way of working through a legal problem.
terms.intermediate: Method is what you fall back on when you do not know the answer. IRAC is one; noting up a case is another.
terms.advanced: Method is transferable across subjects in a way content is not. A reader who can find the current text of a section and check whether a case still stands is not dependent on any particular syllabus.

terms.gloss: A member of the executive with powers given by statute.
terms.intermediate: Ministers make subsidiary legislation and take decisions that statutes assign to them. Those decisions are reviewable for legality.
terms.advanced: A minister's satisfaction clause — *if the Minister is satisfied* — narrows review but does not remove it. The court can still ask whether there was material capable of supporting the satisfaction.

terms.gloss: Ask what defect in the earlier law the Act was passed to cure.
terms.intermediate: A construction guided by the problem the statute was enacted to fix, so that the reading which suppresses the mischief is preferred.
terms.advanced: This is the closest ancestor of s 17A and remains the most useful traditional tool, because it directs attention to the material that establishes purpose: the long title, the preamble, the state of the law before the Act, and the defect it addressed. Where a modern answer says 'purposive', a court is often doing exactly what Heydon's Case described.
terms.source: Heydon's Case (1584); Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967, s 17A

terms.gloss: An untrue assertion that induced the contract, made without knowing it was false.
terms.intermediate: Section 18 covers a positive assertion not warranted by the information of the person making it, though believed true, and certain breaches of duty. Fraud under s 17 is the dishonest counterpart.
terms.advanced: The line between ss 17 and 18 is belief: the maker of a s 18 representation believes it. Both render the agreement voidable under s 19, and the innocent party's right to rescind can be lost by affirmation, lapse of time, or the impossibility of restitution. Section 19's proviso denies avoidance where the party had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, which is a real limit on s 18.

terms.gloss: A belief that is wrong — and sometimes a reason to undo a contract.
terms.intermediate: Not every mistake matters. The law asks whether both sides were wrong about the same fundamental thing, or whether one side simply made a bad bargain.
terms.advanced: Sections 21-23 of the Contracts Act separate a mistake of fact by both parties, which can void the agreement, from a mistake by one party or a mistake of law, which generally does not.

terms.gloss: The duty to take reasonable steps to limit your loss.
terms.intermediate: A claimant cannot recover for loss he could reasonably have avoided. The explanation to s 74 requires the means available for remedying the inconvenience to be taken into account.
terms.advanced: It is not a duty owed to the defendant so much as a limit on recovery, and the standard is reasonableness judged at the time, not with hindsight: a claimant who took a reasonable step that turned out badly still recovers. The burden of showing a failure to mitigate is on the defendant.

terms.gloss: Malayan Law Journal.
terms.intermediate: The main Malaysian series of law reports. In a citation like [2010] 2 MLJ 1, MLJ names the series, 2 the volume and 1 the page.
terms.advanced: Square brackets round the year mean the year is needed to find the volume. Where a case exists in more than one series, cite the report rather than an unreported court-issued judgment, and give the court in brackets at the end.

terms.gloss: Malayan Law Reports, Appellate Courts.
terms.intermediate: A Malaysian report series for appellate decisions. A single case may carry an MLJ, a CLJ and an MLRA citation at once.
terms.advanced: Multiple citations for one judgment are a publishing artefact rather than a sign of importance. Give whichever series your reader can actually reach, and give the court.

terms.gloss: Culpable homicide falling within one of the four limbs of s 300.
terms.intermediate: Section 300 sets out four ways culpable homicide becomes murder, subject to five Exceptions that reduce it back to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
terms.advanced: Limb (c) does most of the work in single-blow cases and asks two questions: did the accused intend to inflict the injury actually inflicted, and is that injury objectively sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The second limb is objective, which is why (c) is often provable where an intention to cause death under (a) is not. The mandatory death penalty was abolished in 2023, so sentencing should never be stated from memory or from an older text.

terms.gloss: Confined to a small compass — of a rule or a reading.
terms.intermediate: A narrow reading of a case restricts it to its facts. It is the main way courts avoid a precedent without overruling it.
terms.advanced: Narrowing is legitimate where the earlier reasoning was tied to facts not present here. Narrowing merely because the result is inconvenient is what per incuriam and overruling exist to do openly.

terms.gloss: The federal statute governing registered land in Peninsular Malaysia.
terms.intermediate: Act 828 as revised in 2020, covering alienation, dealings, charges, caveats and indefeasibility of title.
terms.advanced: Land is a State matter, so a federal Code is possible only through Article 76's uniformity route, and it takes effect in a State on adoption by its legislature. Sabah and Sarawak have their own land legislation and are not a footnote to the Code. The 2020 revision renumbered provisions, so any section cited from an older text must be checked against the current one.
terms.source: National Land Code (Act 828, Revised 2020); Federal Constitution Art 76

terms.gloss: Two rules: hear the other side, and no one a judge in his own cause.
terms.intermediate: The procedural minimum a decision affecting a person must meet. Their content varies with what is at stake and with the statutory framework.
terms.advanced: They are two specific rules, not a general power to require fairness, and an answer should say which one is engaged and what it required on these facts. A decision removing a livelihood attracts far more than a preliminary or investigatory step; an oral hearing, reasons and legal representation are not always required.
terms.source: Standard administrative law as received in Malaysia

terms.gloss: Required — a word that does real work in legal tests.
terms.intermediate: *Necessary* sets a higher bar than useful or desirable. When a test uses it, showing convenience is not enough.
terms.advanced: It also marks the ratio: the reasoning *necessary* to the decision binds, and the rest is obiter. And necessary implication is the only route by which a statute takes away a fundamental right without saying so.

terms.gloss: Careless conduct causing foreseeable damage, in breach of a duty.
terms.intermediate: Four questions in order: duty, breach, causation, remoteness. Each assumes the one before it.
terms.advanced: The order is not stylistic. Arguing remoteness before establishing breach is arguing about nothing, and an answer that opens with the defences has assumed the case it should be proving. Malaysian law has taken its own line in two places worth knowing: the doctor's duty to advise of risks, where Foo Fio Na departed from Bolam, and apportionment for contributory negligence under s 12 of the Civil Law Act 1956.
terms.source: Standard common law; Foo Fio Na v Dr Soo Fook Mun [2007] 1 MLJ 593 (FC); Civil Law Act 1956 s 12

terms.gloss: Anyone so closely affected by what you do that you ought to have them in mind.
terms.intermediate: The word comes from Lord Atkin in Donoghue v Stevenson. It is a test of legal closeness, not of who lives next door.
terms.advanced: The neighbour principle was the original duty test and has since been narrowed. Caparo asks foreseeability, proximity and whether a duty is fair, just and reasonable — the neighbour idea survives inside the first two.

terms.gloss: No one may be a judge in his own cause.
terms.intermediate: The rule against bias. Actual bias need not be shown: the test is objective.
terms.advanced: The working question is whether a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real danger, or real possibility, of bias — and which formulation Malaysian courts currently use is worth checking, because both appear. Pleading actual bias is a tactical error: it is harder to prove and amounts to an allegation of dishonesty the objective test does not require.
terms.source: Standard administrative law; the Malaysian authorities on bias

terms.gloss: The three lists dividing legislative power.
terms.intermediate: List I is Federal, List II is State, List III Concurrent, with supplementary lists for Sabah and Sarawak. Every competence question starts here.
terms.advanced: The counter-intuitive entries are the examinable ones: land and Islamic law are State matters, while civil and criminal law and procedure are federal. That is how a State enactment can regulate Muslim family law while the Penal Code is national — and why the National Land Code, a federal statute on a State subject, needs Article 76 to explain it.

terms.gloss: An offence for which bail is discretionary, not unavailable.
terms.intermediate: Section 388: the court may release the accused on bail. The label misleads almost everyone who meets it for the first time.
terms.advanced: Where the discretion arises the court asks whether the accused will attend trial and whether release creates risks that conditions cannot manage — interference with witnesses, the gravity of the offence and the likely sentence, antecedents and ties to the jurisdiction. Proposing conditions such as sureties, surrender of a passport, or reporting is usually a better answer than asserting that the risk is low.

terms.gloss: A word takes colour from the words around it.
terms.intermediate: The meaning of a term is read in the light of its companions in the provision, rather than in isolation.
terms.advanced: Broader than ejusdem generis, which is really a special case of it: noscitur needs no list of specifics and no genus, only context. It is the canon behind the instruction to read the whole section before the words you came for.

terms.gloss: Knowing something, or being treated by law as knowing it.
terms.intermediate: Notice can be actual (you knew) or constructive (you would have known if you had looked). It also means a formal document telling someone something.
terms.advanced: Under a Torrens system, notice of a prior unregistered interest does not by itself defeat a registered title. That is a deliberate difference from English land law and a common source of error.

terms.gloss: Checking a case's later treatment before relying on it.
terms.intermediate: The step after finding a case: establishing whether it has since been followed, distinguished, doubted or overruled.
terms.advanced: It is the step most often skipped and the one that most often changes the answer. Adorna Properties stood as an available and citable Federal Court decision on indefeasibility for nine years while being wrong, and nothing in the text of the judgment says so.

terms.gloss: A new intervening act that breaks the chain of causation.
terms.intermediate: A later event so independent of the defendant's breach that the law treats it, rather than the breach, as the cause of the damage.
terms.advanced: A deliberate wrongful act by a third party usually breaks the chain; a foreseeable act, or one the defendant's own negligence made likely, usually does not. Ordinary negligent medical treatment following an injury is treated as foreseeable and does not break it, though grossly negligent treatment may. It must be kept distinct from contributory negligence: this defeats the claim, that reduces it.

terms.gloss: A statement not necessary to the decision. Persuasive at most.
terms.intermediate: Anything a judge says that the result did not require. It can be quoted and relied on as persuasive, but it binds nobody.
terms.advanced: A court that expressly declines to decide a point has not decided it, however suggestive its language — reservations of that kind are the most reliably identifiable obiter there is. Considered dicta of a superior court carry real weight in practice, and counsel routinely build arguments on them; the distinction that matters is that a later court is free to disagree without needing any of the machinery for departing from precedent.

terms.gloss: The aim of an agreement or an Act — and, in contract, a ground of invalidity.
terms.intermediate: If the object of an agreement is unlawful, the agreement is void. The object is what the parties were trying to bring about.
terms.advanced: Section 24 of the Contracts Act makes consideration or object void where it is forbidden, defeats a law, is fraudulent, injures a person or property, or is immoral or against public policy.

terms.gloss: Something you are legally bound to do or not do.
terms.intermediate: Obligations come from agreement, from statute, or from the general law of wrongs. Naming the source tells you what happens when it is broken.
terms.advanced: The classical division is contract, tort and unjust enrichment. Malaysian law adds a fourth source in the Contracts Act's quasi-contract provisions, sections 69-73.

terms.gloss: To get something — often by a required procedure.
terms.intermediate: You obtain leave, obtain an order, obtain consent. The word signals that permission or a step is needed first.
terms.advanced: Obtaining by deception is also the core of cheating under section 415 of the Penal Code, where the inducement and the delivery of property are separate elements.
terms.source: Rules of Court 2012; Penal Code, s 415

terms.gloss: Conduct that the law makes punishable.
terms.intermediate: Something a statute says is a crime and attaches a punishment to. An offence has a physical part and usually a mental part, and the prosecution must prove both.
terms.advanced: In Malaysia each offence is defined with its own mental element written into the section, so reasoning from a general English doctrine of mens rea can mislead. The First Schedule to the Criminal Procedure Code then classifies each offence for arrest, investigation and bail.
terms.source: Penal Code; Criminal Procedure Code, First Schedule

terms.gloss: A position with powers attached to the post rather than the person.
terms.intermediate: An officeholder exercises the powers of the office, not their own. When they leave, the powers stay with the post.
terms.advanced: This is why judicial review names the office rather than the individual, and why an act done in a personal capacity by an officeholder is not reviewable at all.

terms.gloss: A person holding an office, public or corporate.
terms.intermediate: Police officers, court officers and company officers all hold defined roles with defined powers. The word signals that duties come from the position.
terms.advanced: In company law *officer* is defined widely and reaches beyond directors, which matters because several offences and duties attach to officers rather than to directors alone.
terms.source: Companies Act 2016, s 2; Criminal Procedure Code

terms.gloss: A person exercising public power, or the version issued by authority.
terms.intermediate: An official act is one done in the role, and it is the role that makes it reviewable. An official copy of a statute is the government's own text.
terms.advanced: Prefer official sources when citing legislation, because unofficial reprints go out of date silently. The Attorney General's Chambers portal is the authoritative text for Malaysian Acts.

terms.gloss: The reverse — often the fastest way to test a rule.
terms.intermediate: Ask what the opposite result would mean. If it is absurd, the rule you have stated is probably too wide.
terms.advanced: The converse of a rule does not follow from it. That a registered proprietor gets an indefeasible title does not mean an unregistered one gets nothing — a caveat and an equitable interest may still exist.

terms.gloss: A member's remedy for being treated unfairly.
terms.intermediate: Section 346: that the company's affairs are being conducted, or the directors' powers exercised, in a manner oppressive to a member or in disregard of a member's interests.
terms.advanced: The complaint is about how the member has been treated, which is what distinguishes it from a derivative action vindicating the company's own right. The court's powers on such a petition are wide and include a buy-out order, which is the outcome most petitions are actually seeking. Pleading oppression and a derivative action together without thought proceeds on inconsistent premises about whose right is in issue.

terms.gloss: Rules of Court 2012 — pleadings.
terms.intermediate: Order 18 governs what a pleading must contain: the material facts relied on, not the evidence and not the law. Fraud and other serious allegations need particulars.
terms.advanced: A party is confined to its pleaded case, and Order 18 rule 19 is the striking-out power. Both are why the pleading is a strategic document rather than a formality.
terms.find: Free at kehakiman.gov.my — Rules of Court 2012 (P.U.(A) 205/2012)

terms.gloss: The judicial review procedure.
terms.intermediate: Requires leave, an applicant who is adversely affected by the decision, and an application made within the prescribed time from when the grounds arose.
terms.advanced: The threshold requirements end more applications than the merits do. The Malaysian standing test — adversely affected — has been stated in the Federal Court and is narrower than the English sufficient interest. The time limit runs from the decision, not from when the applicant gave up on correspondence, so a delay spent writing letters is still delay.
terms.source: Rules of Court 2012 O 53; QSR Brands Bhd v Suruhanjaya Sekuriti [2006] 3 MLJ 164 (CA)

terms.gloss: The court or Land Administrator ordering charged land to be sold.
terms.intermediate: The chargee's remedy on unremedied default. The court will order sale unless the chargor shows cause to the contrary.
terms.advanced: The two tracks — High Court for Registry title, Land Administrator for Land Office title — have different provisions and different appeal routes, and confusing them is the standard error. Because the discretion is narrow, most contested applications are really arguments about whether the statutory notice was valid.
terms.source: National Land Code, the order-for-sale provisions

terms.gloss: The everyday sense of a word, as against a technical one.
terms.intermediate: Courts start with the ordinary meaning of statutory words. They leave it only where the Act defines the word or the context demands otherwise.
terms.advanced: *Ordinary* also marks the standard actor: the ordinary reasonable person in defamation, the ordinary prudent director in company law. Those are legal constructs, not surveys.

terms.gloss: The mode of commencement for a question of law on undisputed facts.
terms.intermediate: Proceeds on affidavit evidence rather than oral testimony, and suits construction questions and applications where the facts are not really in contest.
