terms.advanced: It is unsuitable where credibility is in issue, because affidavits cannot be cross-examined without an order. Some applications must be brought this way by the rules — judicial review being the obvious one — so the choice is not always open.
terms.source: Rules of Court 2012 O 5 and O 7

terms.gloss: In another way — a word that quietly widens a statute.
terms.intermediate: *Or otherwise* at the end of a list usually extends it. How far it extends is settled by the class the earlier words establish.
terms.advanced: This is where ejusdem generis bites: general words after specific ones are read as confined to the same genus, unless the Act shows a wider purpose.

terms.gloss: A provision purporting to exclude the courts' jurisdiction.
terms.intermediate: Statutory wording that says a decision shall be final, or shall not be questioned in any court. Courts construe such clauses narrowly.
terms.advanced: The presumption against ouster is strong enough that clear words are required, and even clear words face a constitutional limit: judicial review of administrative action is inherent in the civil courts, and there is Malaysian authority treating it as part of the basic structure. The practical effect is that an ouster clause is usually read as protecting a decision made within jurisdiction, and as leaving untouched one made outside it.
terms.source: Standard presumption of construction; Malaysian authority on judicial power

terms.gloss: The practical effect of a decision on the parties.
terms.intermediate: The outcome is who won and what they got. It matters to the parties and much less to the law.
terms.advanced: Keep outcome apart from disposal: a successful appeal may still leave a party worse off after a remittal and a costs order.

terms.gloss: A superior court declaring an earlier decision in another case wrong.
terms.intermediate: When a court with the power to do so holds that a previous decision, in a different case, was wrongly decided and should no longer be followed.
terms.advanced: Only a court above the one that decided it can overrule — or, for the Federal Court, itself. Overruling is generally retrospective in effect, which is one reason apex courts do it rarely: it unsettles arrangements made on the faith of the earlier rule. It is routinely confused with reversing, which is a different act entirely.

terms.gloss: To be under an obligation — of money, or of care.
terms.intermediate: You owe a debt and you owe a duty. The word marks that someone else has a corresponding right.
terms.advanced: Duties are owed to particular people, not at large. Identifying to whom the duty was owed is what disposes of most novel negligence claims.

terms.gloss: The largest set of rights the law allows over a thing.
terms.intermediate: An owner can use, exclude, sell and destroy — subject to law. Ownership is a stronger claim than possession, which is only control.
terms.advanced: For land, ownership is defined by the register rather than by the strength of your documents. For goods, title can pass without possession, which is why sale of goods asks separately when property passes and when delivery happens.

terms.gloss: Specific rather than general — and, in pleading, the details relied on.
terms.intermediate: Particulars are the facts that make a bare allegation checkable. Fraud must be pleaded with particulars; a general accusation will be struck out.
terms.advanced: The rule is strict because an allegation of fraud damages a reputation before it is proved. Section 540 of the Companies Act and the Rules of Court both require the specific acts to be identified.

terms.gloss: Someone whose name is on the case — the one suing, or the one being sued.
terms.intermediate: Only a party can win or lose. A witness gives evidence and goes home; a party is bound by the judgment.
terms.advanced: Being a party is what makes res judicata bite, and privity is the contract version of the same idea. Ask early who the parties are, because it decides who can be ordered to do anything.

terms.gloss: Privy Council — the Judicial Committee in London.
terms.intermediate: A London court that used to hear final appeals from Malaysia. Appeals to it were abolished in stages and ended completely in 1985.
terms.advanced: Privy Council decisions on appeal from Malaya remain part of our law and are cited as such. Its decisions on appeal from elsewhere are persuasive only, so the jurisdiction an appeal came from is part of reading the citation.
terms.source: Former final appellate court for Malaysia

terms.gloss: The statute defining offences and the general exceptions.
terms.intermediate: Malaysia's criminal code, derived from the Indian Penal Code. It defines each offence with its own elements and its own mental element.
terms.advanced: Because each offence carries its own fault requirement, the general common law vocabulary of actus reus and mens rea is less useful here than a common law training suggests — you reason from the section, not from a general theory. Section 6 makes every definition subject to the general exceptions in Chapter IV, which is why a homicide answer that never considers private defence has looked at half the picture.

terms.gloss: Decided in ignorance of a statute or binding case that would have changed the result.
terms.intermediate: A decision reached without the court being shown a provision or authority that would have altered the outcome. Such a decision does not bind.
terms.advanced: The doctrine is narrow on purpose. It is not available because the earlier reasoning was poor, or because a later court would have decided differently: the earlier court must have missed something it was obliged to apply, and the omission must have been capable of changing the result. Invoking it loosely is one of the more visible ways to signal that the hierarchy has not been understood.

terms.gloss: Official permission — or, as a verb, to allow.
terms.intermediate: A permit is a licence by another name. It makes lawful what a statute otherwise forbids, on the terms written into it.
terms.advanced: A permit granted by a body acting outside its statutory power is void, and a person prosecuted for acting without one can raise that in defence rather than having to bring a separate review.

terms.gloss: Anything a court may follow but need not.
terms.intermediate: Obiter dicta, decisions of coordinate or lower courts, foreign judgments, and academic writing. Weight depends on the source and the fit, not on any rule.
terms.advanced: In Malaysia the most heavily used persuasive material is English, Indian and Singaporean case law, and its weight turns on whether the statutory scheme is comparable. That qualification does the most work in codified subjects: an English contract case bears on a Malaysian problem only where the Contracts Act 1950 raises the same question, and citing one against the words of a section is worse than citing nothing.

terms.gloss: A group of words read together as a unit.
terms.intermediate: Statutes are read phrase by phrase. A word takes its colour from the words beside it, so pulling one out on its own distorts it.
terms.advanced: That is the basis of noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis: general words following a list are read as limited to the same class. Both are aids, and both yield to clear contrary purpose.

terms.gloss: The person who brings a civil claim.
terms.intermediate: The side that starts a civil case and asks the court for something. In a criminal case the equivalent side is the prosecution, and it is not called a plaintiff.
terms.advanced: The label decides who carries the burden: the plaintiff must prove the facts the claim depends on, so an evenly balanced case is one the plaintiff loses. Where proceedings begin by originating summons the equivalent party is the applicant.

terms.gloss: To set out your case formally — or to answer a criminal charge.
terms.intermediate: In a civil case you plead facts, not evidence and not law. In a criminal case you plead guilty or not guilty to the charge.
terms.advanced: A party is bound by its pleadings and cannot win on a case it never pleaded. Amendments are possible but are discretionary and get harder the later they come.

terms.gloss: The document setting out a party's case in material facts.
terms.intermediate: Plead material facts, not the evidence that will prove them and not the law. The pleadings define the issues the trial will decide.
terms.advanced: Some matters must be pleaded specifically — fraud, misrepresentation, breach of trust, and anything that would take the other side by surprise — and limitation is a defence that must be pleaded, because a court will not take the point for a defendant who has not. A case not pleaded is generally a case that cannot be run at trial.

terms.gloss: The state of the law on a question, or a party's standing in a dispute.
terms.intermediate: *The position in Malaysia* means what our law currently says. It can differ from England even where the wording is identical.
terms.advanced: Always state the local position before the comparative one. English authority is persuasive here and its weight depends on whether a Malaysian statute has occupied the ground.

terms.gloss: Physical control of a thing, with the intention to control it.
terms.intermediate: Possession is two things at once: holding something, and meaning to hold it. Both are needed, which is why a parcel left in your porch is not in your possession until you know it is there.
terms.advanced: Possession does the work of ownership in criminal statutes, where knowledge is the fought-over element, and in landlord and tenant, where exclusive possession marks a lease off from a licence.

terms.gloss: To do with what actually happens, rather than what is theoretically so.
terms.intermediate: Courts care about practical effect: whether a remedy would achieve anything, whether a right can be exercised in fact.
terms.advanced: Practical considerations run through discretion — the balance of convenience for an injunction, futility as an answer to a review, and whether damages would be an adequate remedy.

terms.gloss: The recital of purpose some Acts carry before the enacting words.
terms.intermediate: A statement, where one exists, of what the legislature was trying to achieve. It is admissible evidence of purpose.
terms.advanced: Most modern Malaysian Acts have no preamble and carry their purpose in the long title instead, so an argument that depends on one should first check that it exists. Where there is a preamble it may resolve an ambiguity but cannot cut down clear words in a section — the same limit that applies to the long title.

terms.gloss: An earlier decision used to decide a later case.
terms.intermediate: A precedent binds a lower court on the same point of law. It persuades everywhere else.
terms.advanced: Only the ratio is precedent. The rest of the judgment is obiter, and a precedent can be departed from where it was decided per incuriam or has been overruled.

terms.gloss: Exact — and in law, usually necessary.
terms.intermediate: Precision is not pedantry here. Naming the section, the limb and the party is what makes an argument checkable.
terms.advanced: Imprecision hides errors. *The contract was breached* conceals which term, by which party, and whether the breach went to the root — three questions the remedy depends on.

terms.gloss: A direction about what the court may or must infer.
terms.intermediate: Section 4 distinguishes three: 'may presume' is a discretion, 'shall presume' is mandatory unless disproved, and 'conclusive proof' admits no evidence in rebuttal.
terms.advanced: The three are not interchangeable and the statute's choice of phrase is the whole of the answer to how much room the other side has. Statutory presumptions in drugs and corruption legislation are the practically significant ones, and they are commonly of the 'shall presume' kind, which is what makes them so onerous.

terms.gloss: Statutes are presumed not to operate backwards.
terms.intermediate: A provision is read as applying to the future unless it clearly says otherwise, particularly where it affects vested rights or creates criminal liability.
terms.advanced: The presumption is strongest for substantive provisions and weakest for purely procedural ones, which are often applied to pending proceedings without anybody calling that retrospective. It is displaceable by clear words, and the real argument in a hard case is whether the words are clear enough — and whether the provision is substantive or procedural at all.

terms.gloss: On the face of it — enough unless answered.
terms.intermediate: Used of evidence sufficient to establish a fact in the absence of contrary evidence, and of a case strong enough to require an answer.
terms.advanced: In criminal procedure it has the specific statutory sense under s 180 of the CPC. Outside that it is a general phrase, and using it loosely — 'there is a prima facie breach' — says only that the point is arguable, which is rarely what an answer needs to establish.
terms.source: Criminal Procedure Code s 180; general usage

terms.gloss: The standard at the close of the prosecution case.
terms.intermediate: Section 180 of the CPC: evidence which, if unrebutted, would warrant a conviction. If it is made out the accused is called to enter his defence; if not, he is acquitted.
terms.advanced: The court must undertake a maximum evaluation of the prosecution evidence — testing its credibility rather than merely noting that some evidence exists. The standard at the close of the defence is different and stricter: proof beyond reasonable doubt on the whole of the evidence, with the defence needing only to raise a reasonable doubt rather than to be believed.

terms.gloss: The person an agent acts for.
terms.intermediate: The principal gets the benefit of the agent's authorised acts and carries the burden of them. Do not confuse it with *principle*, a rule.
terms.advanced: An undisclosed principal may generally sue and be sued on a contract the agent made, which is one of the few real inroads on privity.

terms.gloss: The right to defend body or property, within limits.
terms.intermediate: Sections 96 to 106. The right does not extend to inflicting more harm than necessary, and s 100 sets out when defence of the body may extend to causing death.
terms.advanced: Section 99(3) removes the right where there is no reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt and there is time to have recourse to the public authorities. Exceeding the right does not simply lose it: Exception 2 to s 300 reduces murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder where the accused exceeded the right in good faith and without premeditation, which is the difference between two very different sentencing regimes.
terms.source: Penal Code ss 96-106 and Exception 2 to s 300

terms.gloss: Only a party to a contract can sue on it.
terms.intermediate: A person who is not a party acquires no right to enforce the agreement, even if it was made for their benefit.
terms.advanced: Malaysian law keeps privity while relaxing consideration, and holding the two apart is what the s 2(d) point is really testing: consideration may come from a stranger, but a stranger still cannot sue. There is no Malaysian equivalent of the English Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, so the workarounds — agency, trust of a promise, assignment, collateral contract — carry the weight.
terms.source: Contracts Act 1950 s 2(d); Kepong Prospecting Ltd v Schmidt [1968] 1 MLJ 170 (PC)

terms.gloss: About how a case is run, rather than who is right.
terms.intermediate: The machinery: which document starts a case, what the deadlines are, who must disclose what. Most civil disputes are decided on this rather than on the substantive law.
terms.advanced: Treating procedure as the boring administrative part is a mistake people make once. Limitation, striking out and summary judgment end more claims than trials do, and a procedural default is often unrecoverable where a weak case is not.

terms.gloss: The formal steps of a case, from filing to judgment.
terms.intermediate: Proceedings are the case as a process. They can be civil or criminal, and they can be stayed, struck out or discontinued without ever reaching a trial.
terms.advanced: Whether proceedings have been *commenced* fixes the limitation date and engages the court's jurisdiction, so the mode of commencement — writ or originating summons — is a real choice, not a formality.

terms.gloss: A proposal that has been accepted.
terms.intermediate: Once one side proposes something and the other accepts it, the proposal becomes a promise. That is the building block the rest of contract sits on.
terms.advanced: The Act's vocabulary is deliberate: proposal and acceptance are the acts, promise is what they produce, and consideration is the price of the promise. Using English offer-and-acceptance language loosely obscures which step is in dispute.

terms.gloss: In the way the law requires.
terms.intermediate: A power properly exercised is one used for its purpose, on relevant considerations, after a fair procedure. Each of those is separately reviewable.
terms.advanced: *Properly constituted*, *properly served* and *properly pleaded* are technical phrases with defined content. Treating them as loose praise loses the point being made.

terms.gloss: A thing you own, and the bundle of rights that ownership gives you.
terms.intermediate: Lawyers use *property* for the right, not just the object. Two people can hold different property in the same house: an owner and a tenant both have rights, of different shapes.
terms.advanced: Divide it two ways: real property (land and things fixed to it) against personal property, and legal against equitable title. Which division matters depends on the question — a trust splits the second, a lease the first.

terms.gloss: Relative size — and the idea that a response should match what caused it.
terms.intermediate: Proportion appears in apportioning blame between parties and in asking whether a restriction goes further than necessary.
terms.advanced: Contributory negligence reduces damages in proportion to responsibility. Proportionality in public law is a different tool, testing whether a limit on a right is no more than needed.
terms.source: Civil Law Act 1956, s 12; constitutional law

terms.gloss: Asking whether a restriction goes further than its purpose requires.
terms.intermediate: A test that examines whether a limit on a right is suitable, necessary, and balanced against what it achieves — rather than merely whether it falls within a permitted category.
terms.advanced: Its status in Malaysia is contested and should be stated as such: it has been accepted in the constitutional context, argued through Art 8(1), and its standing as a free-standing head of administrative review is a separate question that should be checked against current authority rather than assumed. An answer that applies it as settled law overstates the position; one that ignores it understates it.
terms.source: Sivarasa Rasiah v Badan Peguam Malaysia [2010] 2 MLJ 333 (FC); the Malaysian case law on Art 8(1)

terms.gloss: What English law calls an offer.
terms.intermediate: Signifying to another your willingness to do or abstain from something, with a view to obtaining that other's assent. Section 2(a).
terms.advanced: The vocabulary matters because the Act uses proposal, acceptance and promisor throughout, and an answer written in the English vocabulary reads as though the Act had not been opened. A proposal must be distinguished from an invitation to treat, which is not a proposal at all and cannot be accepted into a contract.

terms.gloss: A statement of law that a case is said to support.
terms.intermediate: When you cite a case you cite it *for* a proposition. Make sure the case actually decided that, rather than merely mentioning it.
terms.advanced: The commonest citation failure is stating a proposition wider than the ratio supports. Narrow the proposition to what was necessary to the decision, then argue the extension separately.

terms.gloss: The person named on the register as owner of land.
terms.intermediate: Whoever the land register says owns the land. Long occupation, family history and a document in a drawer do not make somebody the proprietor.
terms.advanced: The register is the title, so the proprietor is the owner even against someone with a better moral claim — subject to the exceptions in s 340(2), which is where fraud and forgery are argued.

terms.gloss: The side bringing a criminal charge, in the name of the State.
terms.intermediate: The State's side of a criminal case. It must prove the offence beyond reasonable doubt, and it carries that burden from the first witness to the last.
terms.advanced: The power to institute, conduct and discontinue criminal proceedings belongs to the Public Prosecutor and is a constitutional discretion rather than an ordinary administrative one. A person who makes a police report does not thereby become the prosecutor.
terms.source: Federal Constitution Art 145(3); Criminal Procedure Code

terms.gloss: To satisfy the court that something is true, to the required standard.
terms.intermediate: Proving is not asserting. You prove a fact by evidence the court accepts, at the standard the case demands — the balance of probabilities in a civil case, beyond reasonable doubt in a criminal one.
terms.advanced: Keep proof apart from the burden. The burden says who must prove; the standard says how convincingly. Section 101 of the Evidence Act answers the first, not the second.

terms.gloss: Of a statute: to lay down. What it says is a provision.
terms.intermediate: When a section provides for something, that is the law until it is amended or repealed. Read the words, not the summary of them.
terms.advanced: *Provided that* introduces a proviso, which cuts down what came before it. A proviso is construed narrowly and against the section it qualifies, not as a free-standing rule.

terms.gloss: A particular part of an Act — a section, subsection or paragraph.
terms.intermediate: One piece of a statute, small enough to quote. When you are asked what the law is, the answer usually starts by naming the provision.
terms.advanced: Read a provision in its place: the Part it sits in, the sections around it, and any definition section or proviso that qualifies it. A clause read alone is the commonest source of a confident wrong answer.

terms.gloss: A qualification attached to the provision it sits under.
terms.intermediate: A clause beginning 'Provided that…' which cuts down or excepts something from the rule stated immediately before it.
terms.advanced: A proviso is read with its principal provision, not as a free-standing rule, and it is generally construed as doing no more than its words require. The classic student error is to quote a sub-section and stop, having missed a proviso that qualifies precisely the situation in the facts.

terms.gloss: The office with control of all criminal prosecutions.
terms.intermediate: The Attorney General, acting as Public Prosecutor, has discretion under Article 145(3) to institute, conduct or discontinue any criminal proceedings.
terms.advanced: The consequence is that a prosecution is not the complainant's to withdraw: forgiveness may end a civil suit and does not end a charge, though in practice it may influence whether one is continued. The discretion is very broad and the grounds on which it can be reviewed are narrow, which is a recurring topic in administrative law answers.

terms.gloss: To communicate something to at least one other person.
terms.intermediate: In defamation, publication is what makes a statement actionable. Saying it only to the person it is about is not publication.
terms.advanced: Every repetition is a fresh publication with its own limitation period, which is why forwarding a message can create liability where the original author's claim has expired.

terms.gloss: What the law imposes on a person convicted of an offence.
terms.intermediate: Punishment follows conviction and is a separate stage with its own principles. Guilt is about the past; sentence looks at the offender as well as the offence.
terms.advanced: A mandatory sentence removes the court's discretion entirely, which is why the classification of an offence can matter more to the outcome than anything argued at trial.

terms.gloss: What a provision was meant to achieve.
terms.intermediate: Reading for purpose means asking what problem Parliament was solving. It is now the starting point in Malaysia, not a last resort.
terms.advanced: Section 17A of the Interpretation Acts requires a construction promoting the purpose to be preferred. Purpose is found in the Act itself first — long title, preamble, scheme — before external material.

terms.gloss: Prefer the reading that promotes the Act's purpose. In Malaysia this is statutory.
terms.intermediate: Where a provision can bear more than one meaning, the court prefers the one that advances the object underlying the Act. Section 17A of the Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967 makes this a direction, not a choice.
terms.advanced: Section 17A operates on constructions the words can bear; it does not authorise a reading the language cannot support, and it does not licence rewriting a provision that admits of only one meaning. The practical consequence for an answer is an order of work: show the words are capable of two readings, then use purpose to choose. Starting at purpose is the most common error in the subject, and it comes from working out of English textbooks written before any equivalent direction existed there.

terms.gloss: A protected occasion, defeated by malice.
terms.intermediate: Where the maker of a statement has a duty or interest in making it and the recipient a corresponding interest in receiving it, the statement is protected unless malice is shown.
terms.advanced: Reciprocity is the requirement people forget: a duty to speak is not enough without a corresponding interest in the listener. Whether the Reynolds line of responsible-journalism privilege forms part of Malaysian law has been argued here and should not be assumed either way — if an answer needs it, it needs a Malaysian citation.
terms.source: Standard common law; the Malaysian authorities on privilege

terms.gloss: As much as it is worth — payment for value conferred.
terms.intermediate: A claim for reasonable remuneration where work has been done but no price is fixed by an enforceable contract.
terms.advanced: It sits partly in contract, where the parties simply left the price open, and partly in restitution, where the contract was void, discharged or never formed. In Malaysia the restitutionary side is largely handled by ss 65, 66 and 71 of the Contracts Act rather than by an unwritten law of unjust enrichment, so the section should be identified rather than the label used alone.

terms.gloss: The set of outcomes a decision-maker could lawfully reach.
terms.intermediate: Review asks whether the decision was inside the range, not whether it was the best point in it. Two different decisions can both be lawful.
terms.advanced: The range idea is what makes Wednesbury a boundary rather than a merits test. It is also why proportionality is more intrusive: it asks about the point chosen within the range, not just the range.

terms.gloss: The rule the decision actually rests on — the binding part.
terms.intermediate: The proposition of law a court applied to the material facts in order to reach its result. Everything else in the judgment, however well written, is not binding.
terms.advanced: The test is necessity, not emphasis: if the outcome would stand without the proposition, it is not ratio. The hard part is not identifying it but stating it at the right level of generality — too narrow and it governs no later case, too broad and you have made the court decide something it did not. Where several judgments are given, the ratio is what commanded a majority, which may be narrower than any single judgment.

terms.gloss: The stated basis for a decision.
terms.intermediate: Courts give reasons so the losing side knows why and so higher courts can check. Reasons are also where the law for future cases is made.
terms.advanced: A duty to give reasons is not universal in Malaysian administrative law, but absence of reasons can support an inference that there were none that were good — and inadequate reasons can themselves be a ground of review.

terms.gloss: The chain of steps that gets from the rule to the result.
terms.intermediate: Reasoning is what you follow when you read a case, and what you must produce in an answer. The conclusion alone earns nothing.
terms.advanced: Legal reasoning is mostly analogy and distinction rather than deduction. Two cases are alike for legal purposes when they are alike in the respects the rule makes relevant, which is an argument rather than an observation.

terms.gloss: Bringing something back from memory without being shown it.
terms.intermediate: Recall is harder than recognition and worth much more. If you can only recognise a rule, you do not yet know it.
terms.advanced: Free recall under retrieval conditions is what predicts later performance. That is the design principle behind testing yourself before rereading, and behind spaced review.

terms.gloss: How and how far English law became part of Malaysian law.
terms.intermediate: By statute, to fixed dates, subject to local circumstances and displaced by local legislation. It is not a general rule that English law applies.
terms.advanced: The practical test in an answer is whether a Malaysian statute occupies the field. Contract, criminal law and evidence are codified, so the starting point is the Act and English cases are illustration at most; land is governed by the Code with English land law expressly excluded. Where nothing local governs — much of tort — received common law does the work.

terms.gloss: The official written material a court produced or considered.
terms.intermediate: An appeal is decided on the record: the pleadings, the evidence and the judgment. New material is admitted only exceptionally.
terms.advanced: An error of law on the face of the record was historically the only defect certiorari could reach. That limit has gone, but the phrase survives in judgments and needs recognising.

terms.gloss: To get back, through a court, what you are owed.
terms.intermediate: Recovery is the practical end of a claim. A judgment you cannot enforce has recovered nothing.
terms.advanced: Ask early whether the defendant can pay. A claim against a company with no assets and a claim against its solvent director are different claims, and the corporate veil is what stands between them.

terms.gloss: A fall in share value that merely mirrors the company's loss.
terms.intermediate: Where a wrong to the company reduces the value of every member's shares, the claim belongs to the company and a member cannot sue for the diminution personally.
terms.advanced: The rule prevents double recovery and preserves the priority of the company's creditors. Its practical effect is to force an unhappy member into the derivative action or the oppression petition, which is why identifying whose loss it is comes before choosing a remedy.
terms.source: Standard company law; Companies Act 2016 ss 346-350

terms.gloss: The official list of who owns what land, kept by the state.
terms.intermediate: Malaysia records land ownership in a government register. The register is not evidence of ownership — it *is* ownership. Your name on it makes you the owner; your name off it means you are not, whatever your papers say.
terms.advanced: This is the Torrens system, given effect by the National Land Code. Registration confers title rather than recording it, which is why forgery cases turn on section 340 rather than on who signed what.

terms.gloss: Entered on the official register — and so, for land, actually owned.
terms.intermediate: A registered interest is one the state has written down. For land that word does the heavy lifting: an unregistered buyer with a signed contract does not own the land yet.
terms.advanced: Distinguish a registered interest from a registrable one. A caveat protects the second while the first is being obtained; it does not create the first.

terms.gloss: Entering a dealing or a body on an official register.
terms.intermediate: The formal step that makes something official. For land it is the moment ownership passes; for a company it is the moment the company exists as a person.
terms.advanced: Under the National Land Code registration is what creates title rather than merely recording it, which is why a signed agreement leaves the buyer with contractual rights and no title until the transfer is registered.

terms.gloss: Letting someone go, or giving up a claim against them.
terms.intermediate: A person is released from custody; a party is released from a liability. In the second sense a release ends the claim for good.
terms.advanced: A release given to one joint wrongdoer can discharge the others, while a covenant not to sue does not. Which document was signed decides who is still exposed.

terms.gloss: The gate: a fact is admissible only because a section makes it relevant.
terms.intermediate: Sections 6 to 55 declare categories of relevant fact — same transaction, cause or effect, motive and conduct, admissions and confessions, statements of persons who cannot be called, and others.
terms.advanced: Relevancy under the Act is a legal category, not a measure of probative value, so evidence can be plainly probative and still inadmissible because no section reaches it. Keep it separate from burden: first ask whether the evidence goes in under a named section, then ask who has to prove what and to what standard.

terms.gloss: Belief and practice — protected by Article 11, and limited by it.
terms.intermediate: Article 11 gives the right to profess and practise a religion. Islam has a special constitutional position, and state law may control propagation among Muslims.
terms.advanced: Article 11(5) subjects the right to public order, health and morality, and Article 121(1A) removes matters within syariah jurisdiction from the civil courts. Most hard cases are jurisdictional before they are substantive.

terms.gloss: To act on something said or done by another.
terms.intermediate: Reliance turns a statement into a legal problem. A misrepresentation matters because someone relied on it and entered the contract.
terms.advanced: Reliance is also the engine of estoppel and legitimate expectation: the promise or practice is protected because someone reasonably ordered their affairs around it.

terms.gloss: Detention authorised by a Magistrate for the purpose of investigation.
terms.intermediate: An arrested person may not be held beyond twenty-four hours without a Magistrate's order under s 117 of the CPC. The maximum periods are graduated by the sentence the offence carries.
terms.advanced: The twenty-four hour limit is constitutional, in Art 5(4), not merely statutory. A remand hearing is a real hearing: the police must show why further detention is needed, and the Magistrate sets the period thought fit within the statutory maximum. Those maxima have been amended, so they should be taken from the current text.
terms.source: Criminal Procedure Code s 117; Federal Constitution Art 5(4)

terms.gloss: What a court can actually give you.
terms.intermediate: The thing you are asking the court for: money, an order to do something, an order to stop, or a statement of where the parties stand. A right with no remedy attached is of little practical use.
terms.advanced: Ask what remedy the client wants before choosing the cause of action, because remedies differ in availability: damages are as of right once liability is shown, while specific performance and injunctions are discretionary and equitable.

terms.gloss: Liability only for damage of a foreseeable kind.
terms.intermediate: The kind of damage must be reasonably foreseeable; the precise manner of its occurrence and its extent need not be.
terms.advanced: The eggshell skull principle sits inside this rather than beside it: foreseeability governs the type of injury, and the claimant's particular susceptibility governs how bad it turns out to be without reducing the claim. In contract the equivalent limit is s 74 of the Contracts Act, and the two should not be run together — the contractual test looks at what the parties contemplated when contracting.
terms.source: The Wagon Mound (No 1) [1961] AC 388; Contracts Act 1950 s 74 for the contractual analogue

terms.gloss: A statement of fact made to get someone to act.
terms.intermediate: A representation induces the contract; a term is part of it. Breaking a term is breach, and a false representation is misrepresentation.
terms.advanced: The remedies differ sharply. Misrepresentation leads to rescission and, under section 19 of the Contracts Act, a voidable contract; breach of a term leads to damages and sometimes termination.

terms.gloss: Conduct showing an intention no longer to be bound.
terms.intermediate: A refusal to perform, or disabling oneself from performing, in a way that entitles the innocent party to treat the contract as at an end.
terms.advanced: It puts the innocent party to an election: terminate and sue, or affirm and keep the contract alive. The election must be made within a reasonable time and once made is irrevocable, and affirming means the contract remains on foot for both parties — including any obligations the affirming party would rather not perform.

terms.gloss: The thing speaks for itself.
terms.intermediate: Where an accident is of a kind that does not ordinarily happen without negligence, and the thing was under the defendant's control, the court may infer negligence.
terms.advanced: It is an evidential aid rather than a rule of law, and its effect is contested: on the better view it permits an inference rather than reversing the legal burden. A defendant answers it by showing how the accident happened without negligence, or that reasonable care was in fact taken.

terms.gloss: A matter already decided cannot be litigated again.
terms.intermediate: Once a court of competent jurisdiction has finally determined an issue between the parties, neither may reopen it in later proceedings.
terms.advanced: It covers both the cause of action and, in its issue estoppel form, particular issues necessarily decided. The related doctrine in Henderson v Henderson extends it to points that could and should have been raised in the earlier proceedings, which is why splitting a case across two actions is dangerous.
terms.source: Standard common law; Evidence Act 1950 ss 40-43

terms.gloss: Unwinding a contract and putting the parties back where they were.
terms.intermediate: The remedy that follows avoidance of a voidable contract: the contract is treated as at an end and benefits are restored.
terms.advanced: It is barred where restitutio in integrum is impossible, where the innocent party has affirmed, after undue delay, or where third-party rights have intervened. Section 65 of the Contracts Act deals with the consequences of rescission, and s 66 with restoration of advantages under agreements discovered to be void.

terms.gloss: Finding the law that governs a question, and checking it is still good.
terms.intermediate: Research is two jobs: finding the source, and confirming it has not been amended, overruled or distinguished away.
terms.advanced: Skipping the second job is the characteristic beginner's failure. A repealed section and a current one look identical on the page.

terms.gloss: A decision formally passed at a meeting.
terms.intermediate: A decision taken by a vote — of the members, or of the board. How many votes it needs depends on which kind of resolution it is.
terms.advanced: Procedure is not a formality here: notice, quorum and the majority required are conditions of validity, and an irregularity may either be curable or invalidate the resolution outright. Which of the two it is turns on whether the requirement protects the company or the individual member.

terms.gloss: The party answering an appeal or an application.
terms.intermediate: The side defending the decision on appeal, or answering an application. Which side that is depends on who lost below.
terms.advanced: Also the answering party in proceedings begun by originating summons, and in judicial review, where the respondent is the public body whose decision is challenged.
terms.source: Courts of Judicature Act 1964; Rules of Court 2012

terms.gloss: A limit written into a title, or into a right.
terms.intermediate: Land titles can carry a restriction in interest — the owner cannot sell or charge without someone's consent. It sits on the title and binds whoever holds it.
terms.advanced: A restriction in interest is distinct from an express condition and from a caveat. It limits dealing rather than use, and a dealing entered in breach of it is liable to be rejected at the registry.

terms.gloss: What happened at the end — the outcome, not the reasoning.
terms.intermediate: Two cases can reach the same result for different reasons. It is the reasons that bind, so never argue from the result alone.
terms.advanced: A result-only reading is what produces the classic misuse of authority: citing a case for a proposition it never decided, because the outcome happened to suit.

terms.gloss: Trying to recall, and checking — the thing that actually builds memory.
terms.intermediate: Attempting to produce an answer from memory, then verifying it. It beats re-reading by a wide margin, even when the attempt fails.
terms.advanced: The counter-intuitive part is that difficulty is the mechanism, not a side effect: a struggle that ends in a correct check does more than a fluent pass over the text. Fluency during study is a poor guide to later recall, which is why revision that feels smooth should be treated with suspicion.
terms.source: Make It Stick; the retrieval practice literature

terms.gloss: An appeal court setting aside the decision below in the same case.
terms.intermediate: What happens when an appeal succeeds: the higher court substitutes its own outcome for the one reached below, in the very same proceedings.
terms.advanced: Reversing operates on the parties before the court; overruling operates on the law for everybody. A decision can be reversed on appeal without any point of law being overruled — the appeal court may simply take a different view of the facts or the exercise of a discretion.

terms.gloss: Withdrawing a proposal before it is accepted.
terms.intermediate: A proposal may be revoked at any time before communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer, but not afterwards. Section 5(1).
terms.advanced: Because the cut-off is the moment fixed by s 4(2)(a), a posted acceptance can beat a revocation that was posted first. A promise to hold an offer open is not binding without consideration, which means the proposer could have revoked in time — not that they did, and checking the timing under ss 4 and 5 comes before any of that.

terms.gloss: The chance that something will go wrong, and who carries it.
terms.intermediate: Law allocates risk. Contracts do it by their terms; tort does it by asking who should have guarded against the harm.
terms.advanced: In sale of goods, risk usually passes with property rather than with delivery, so goods destroyed after property passes are the buyer's loss even though they never arrived.

terms.gloss: The rules governing civil proceedings in the High Court and subordinate courts.
terms.intermediate: They set out how an action is begun, pleaded, disposed of before trial, tried and enforced — Order by Order.
terms.advanced: Procedure is not administrative detail: most civil cases end on an interlocutory application rather than at trial, so the Orders governing summary judgment, striking out and injunctions decide more disputes than the substantive law does. Order 53 is the judicial review procedure and is the one most likely to be missed in a public law answer.

terms.gloss: Supreme Court — in Indian citations, India's highest court.
terms.intermediate: In a citation like AIR 1958 SC 465, SC is the Supreme Court of India. Malaysia had a Supreme Court too, between 1985 and 1994, before it became the Federal Court.
terms.advanced: Read the series before the court abbreviation: AIR points to India, so SC there is not a Malaysian court. Malaysian decisions from 1985 to 1994 cite the Supreme Court as our own apex, which is the same institution the Federal Court now is.
terms.source: Indian and former Malaysian court hierarchies

terms.gloss: The overall design of an Act — how its parts fit together.
terms.intermediate: Reading the scheme means seeing what the Act is trying to do as a whole, not just the section in front of you.
terms.advanced: Scheme is a legitimate and internal aid to construction, and it usually settles ambiguity before any external material is needed. Read the long title, the arrangement of parts, and the definitions together.

terms.gloss: Contracts Act 1950 s 10 — what turns an agreement into a contract.
terms.intermediate: Four requirements: free consent, parties competent to contract, a lawful consideration and a lawful object. Fail any one and there is no contract.
terms.advanced: Each limb opens onto its own body of law — consent onto the vitiating factors in s 14, capacity onto s 11, lawful object onto s 24. An answer asserting a contract exists without naming the limb in issue has skipped the analysis.

terms.gloss: Penal Code — when private defence of the body extends to causing death.
terms.intermediate: The right of private defence exists first; section 100 says how far it goes. Only in the listed situations does it extend to causing death.
terms.advanced: Reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt is the commonest of the listed grounds. The apprehension must be reasonable and the response proportionate — the right ends when the threat does.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Penal Code (Act 574)

terms.gloss: Evidence Act 1950 s 101 — whoever asserts must prove.
terms.intermediate: Anyone who wants the court to give judgment on a right that depends on facts must prove those facts. If neither side calls evidence, the person asserting loses.
terms.advanced: Read with s 102, which asks who would fail if no evidence at all were given — a practical test for locating the legal burden. Section 103 then puts the burden on any particular fact on the person who wants the court to believe it.

terms.gloss: Evidence Act 1950 s 102 — on whom the burden lies.
terms.intermediate: The burden sits with the person who would fail if no evidence were given on either side. Picture an empty trial and ask who walks out disappointed.
terms.advanced: Sections 101 and 102 describe the legal burden, which does not move. The evidential burden — the practical need to answer now — shifts back and forth and is a different thing; saying only that 'the burden shifted' hides which one you mean.

terms.gloss: Evidence Act 1950 — the burden of proving any particular fact.
terms.intermediate: Section 103 puts the burden of a particular fact on whoever wants the court to believe it. It works fact by fact, inside a case whose overall burden section 101 has already placed.
terms.advanced: Sections 101 and 102 describe the legal burden — who loses if nothing is proved. Section 103 is doing something narrower, and confusing the two produces the common error of arguing that the burden has *shifted*. It is named in full here on purpose: the bare number is used in this app for more than one Act, so it is not auto-linked in prose. Look it up by name rather than expecting a hover.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Evidence Act 1950 (Act 56)

terms.gloss: The accused must prove a general exception.
terms.intermediate: Where an accused relies on a general exception in the Penal Code, or a special exception or proviso in the law defining the offence, the burden of proving the circumstances is on him and the court presumes their absence.
terms.advanced: This is a genuine legal burden, discharged on the balance of probabilities — not merely an evidential one, and not the English position on many defences. An answer that says the accused must 'raise' the exception and the prosecution must then disprove it beyond reasonable doubt has stated the wrong rule for this jurisdiction.

terms.gloss: A fact especially within a person's knowledge is for him to prove.
terms.intermediate: Where a fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon him.
terms.advanced: The most over-used provision in the Act. It reaches a specific fact peculiarly within someone's knowledge — a licence, an authority, a reason for being somewhere — and cannot be used to reverse the general burden or to relieve the prosecution of proving its case. Deploying it to shift the whole case is a misreading that is easy for a marker to spot.

terms.gloss: Criminal Procedure Code s 117 — remand beyond twenty-four hours.
terms.intermediate: Detention past the first twenty-four hours needs a Magistrate's order, made for the investigation and for the period the Magistrate thinks fit. The police cannot extend it themselves.
terms.advanced: The hearing is short and often in a small room, and it is meant to be a real check rather than a formality: the investigating officer must say why more time is needed, and the person arrested may be heard.

terms.gloss: Civil Law Act 1956 — damages are reduced for the claimant's own share of the blame.
terms.intermediate: Where a claimant is partly responsible for their own damage, section 12 lets the court reduce the award to what is just and equitable. It does not defeat the claim.
terms.advanced: Apportionment replaced the old rule that contributory negligence was a complete defence. The reduction is by share of responsibility, which takes in both blameworthiness and causal potency, not by arithmetic on the injuries.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Civil Law Act 1956 (Act 67)

terms.gloss: Contracts Act 1950 — what makes consent free.
terms.intermediate: Section 14 says consent is free when it is not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake. Those five are the whole list.
terms.advanced: It is a closed list, and sections 15 to 23 supply the statutory definitions. Do not import English vitiating doctrines that do not fit one of the five — the statute has occupied the ground.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136)

terms.gloss: The provision making the purposive approach statutory in Malaysia.
terms.intermediate: Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967 s 17A: a construction promoting the purpose or object underlying the Act is to be preferred to one that does not.
terms.advanced: Its existence is why the English hierarchy of literal, golden and mischief rules is a description of tools rather than a sequence to be worked through here. The older rules survive as ways of getting at meaning — the mischief rule in particular is s 17A's closest ancestor — but the starting point is the section, and an argument that never reaches it has skipped the governing provision.

terms.gloss: Contracts Act 1950 — the contract is voidable where consent was not free.
terms.intermediate: Where consent was caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, section 19 makes the agreement voidable at the option of the party wronged.
terms.advanced: Voidable, not void: the contract stands until it is rescinded, and the right to rescind can be lost by affirmation, delay, or third-party rights. Mistake under section 21 is the different case, and makes the agreement void.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136)

terms.gloss: Contracts Act 1950 s 2 — the definitions the whole Act runs on.
terms.intermediate: Where proposal, acceptance, promise, agreement and consideration are each defined. Contract questions start here, because the Act's vocabulary is not the English one.
terms.advanced: The steps are deliberate: s 2(a) proposal, 2(b) acceptance turning it into a promise, 2(d) consideration, 2(e) agreement. Naming which step is in dispute is most of a formation answer, and s 2(d) is what lets past consideration count here where English law would not.

terms.gloss: Contracts Act 1950 — a shared mistake of fact makes the agreement void.
terms.intermediate: Section 21 applies where both parties are mistaken about a matter of fact essential to the agreement. The agreement is void from the start.
terms.advanced: Void, not voidable, so there is no election to make and nothing to rescind. Compare section 22: a mistake by one party alone does not make the agreement voidable on that ground.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136)

terms.gloss: Companies Act 2016 s 213 — the core duties of a director.
terms.intermediate: Two duties. Under 213(1) a director must exercise powers for a proper purpose and in good faith in the best interest of the company. Under 213(2) they must exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence.
terms.advanced: The care standard has a floor set by the office and rises for a director who happens to know more, so an accountant on the board is held higher. The duty is owed to the company, not to individual shareholders, which decides who may sue.

terms.gloss: Companies Act 2016 — the business judgement rule.
terms.intermediate: Section 214 shelters a director who makes a business judgement in good faith, for a proper purpose, without a material personal interest, on reasonable information, and rationally believing it to be in the company's best interest.
terms.advanced: It is a shelter for the *judgement*, not for the process. Each condition must be met, and the fifth is judged rationally rather than reasonably — a low bar, but not an absent one.
terms.find: Free at ssm.com.my and lom.agc.gov.my — Companies Act 2016 (Act 777)

terms.gloss: Companies Act 2016 — improper use of the company's property, position or information.
terms.intermediate: A director must not use the company's property, position, opportunity or information to gain an advantage or to cause the company detriment.
terms.advanced: This is the statutory form of the no-conflict and no-profit rules. It bites even where the company could not have taken the opportunity itself, which is what makes it stricter than an ordinary loyalty test.
terms.find: Free at ssm.com.my and lom.agc.gov.my — Companies Act 2016 (Act 777)

terms.gloss: Contracts Act 1950 s 24 — when consideration or object is unlawful.
terms.intermediate: Lists what makes the price or the purpose of a deal unlawful: forbidden by law, defeating any law, fraudulent, injurious to person or property, or immoral or against public policy. If it falls in, the whole agreement is void.
terms.advanced: Do not reach for illegality as one general doctrine. Section 24 sets out categories and s 25 deals with an agreement only partly unlawful, so the analysis is which category and what survives, not whether the court disapproves.

terms.gloss: Agreements without consideration are void — with three exceptions.
terms.intermediate: The exceptions are (a) writing and registration, natural love and affection, parties in a near relation; (b) a promise to compensate a past voluntary act done for the promisor; and (c) a written, signed promise to pay a time-barred debt.
terms.advanced: Limb (a) is the one most often stated incompletely: writing alone is not enough, registration is required too. Limb (b) is the safe route for the spontaneous good turn, and limb (c) needs a debt actually barred by limitation rather than merely unpaid. Because the Act supplies a formality, reaching for intention to create legal relations instead is the wrong answer even when it produces the right outcome.

terms.gloss: Criminal Procedure Code — the rights of a person arrested.
terms.intermediate: Section 28A requires the arrested person to be told why, and gives the right to contact a relative or friend and to consult a lawyer of their choice.
terms.advanced: The rights may be deferred where the police believe compliance would compromise the investigation, and that exception is where the litigation is. Article 5(3) of the Constitution stands behind the section and is not limited by it.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593)

terms.gloss: Penal Code — the definition of culpable homicide.
terms.intermediate: Section 299 defines culpable homicide: causing death by an act done with the intention of causing death, or of causing bodily injury likely to cause death, or with knowledge that it is likely to cause death.
terms.advanced: Every murder is culpable homicide; not every culpable homicide is murder. Section 300 lifts it, and the exceptions to section 300 bring it back down to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Penal Code (Act 574)

terms.gloss: Civil Law Act 1956 s 3 — the reception of English law.
terms.intermediate: Malaysian courts apply English common law and equity as they stood at stated cut-off dates, and only so far as local circumstances permit. It is a limited reception, not an open door.
terms.advanced: Two limits do the work: the date, which freezes what was received, and the local-circumstances proviso, which lets a court decline an English rule that does not suit. Later English decisions are persuasive only, and citing one as though it were binding is the standard error.

terms.gloss: Penal Code s 300 — when culpable homicide is murder.
terms.intermediate: Sets out the four limbs that raise culpable homicide to murder, and the Exceptions that bring it back down. Establish culpable homicide under s 299 first.
terms.advanced: Going straight to s 300 because someone died inverts the structure and usually picks the wrong limb. Section 300(c) is close to a rule rather than a standard: did you intend the injury, and would an injury like that normally kill.

terms.gloss: Penal Code — the punishment for murder.
terms.intermediate: Section 302 sets the sentence for murder. Since 2023 the death penalty for it is no longer mandatory.
terms.advanced: The conviction and the sentence are separate questions. Reducing murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder moves the case from section 302 to section 304, which is a different sentencing range entirely.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Penal Code (Act 574)

terms.gloss: Penal Code — the punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
terms.intermediate: Section 304 is where a killing lands when an exception to section 300 applies, or when the mental element for murder is not made out.
terms.advanced: It has two limbs with different maxima, turning on whether the act was done with intention or only with knowledge. Which limb applies is argued at sentence and is often the real contest once the exception is accepted.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Penal Code (Act 574)

terms.gloss: National Land Code — who may lodge a private caveat.
terms.intermediate: Not everybody may caveat. Section 323 lists who can: broadly, a person claiming title or a registrable interest, and certain others the Code names.
terms.advanced: A caveat lodged without a caveatable interest is liable to be removed with compensation payable. The claim must be to an interest in the land itself, not merely a contractual right against the proprietor.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — National Land Code (Act 828)

terms.gloss: National Land Code s 340 — indefeasibility of registered title.
terms.intermediate: Registered title is indefeasible, subject to the exceptions in s 340(2) — fraud, forgery and an instrument that was void or insufficient. The register is the title, not merely evidence of it.
terms.advanced: Whether a purchaser from a forger takes good title is the immediate-versus-deferred question. Adorna Properties read it as immediate for nine years; Tan Ying Hong departed from that in 2010 and restored deferred indefeasibility.

terms.gloss: Penal Code — the definition of theft.
terms.intermediate: Theft is taking movable property out of someone's possession, dishonestly, without their consent. The property never has to have been handed over.
terms.advanced: Theft, criminal breach of trust and cheating are told apart by how possession was obtained: never given, given lawfully then misappropriated, or given because of a deception. That branching answers most property-offence problems.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Penal Code (Act 574)

terms.gloss: Criminal Procedure Code — bail in bailable offences.
terms.intermediate: Where the offence is bailable, section 387 makes release on bail a right rather than a favour. The court sets the amount and the conditions.
terms.advanced: Read it with section 388, which governs non-bailable offences and makes release discretionary. The classification comes from the First Schedule, so the schedule decides the argument before it starts.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593)

terms.gloss: Contracts Act 1950 — when a communication is complete.
terms.intermediate: Section 4 fixes the moment a proposal, an acceptance or a revocation takes effect. Formation problems are usually decided by these timings rather than by what the parties meant.
terms.advanced: Acceptance is complete against the proposer when it is put in a course of transmission, and against the acceptor only when it comes to the proposer's knowledge. That gap is deliberate, and it is what section 5 then works against.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136)

terms.gloss: Penal Code — the definition of criminal breach of trust.
terms.intermediate: Section 405 covers a person entrusted with property who then misappropriates it or uses it against the terms of the trust. The property was handed over lawfully.
terms.advanced: Entrustment is the element that separates it from theft, and dishonest misappropriation the element that separates it from a mere civil breach. Both must be proved; a broken promise is not enough.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Penal Code (Act 574)

terms.gloss: Penal Code s 415 — cheating.
terms.intermediate: Delivery of property induced by deception. What separates it from theft and criminal breach of trust is how possession was obtained: never given, given lawfully, or given by a trick.
terms.advanced: Ask the possession question before naming the offence. Theft under s 378 is property moved out of possession without consent; criminal breach of trust under s 405 is property entrusted and then misappropriated; cheating is consent obtained by deception.

terms.gloss: Contracts Act 1950 — when a proposal or acceptance may still be revoked.
terms.intermediate: Section 5 gives the deadline. A proposal can be revoked until the acceptance is complete as against the proposer; after that it is too late.
terms.advanced: Read section 5(1) beside section 4(2): the revocation window closes at the moment of posting, not at the moment of receipt, so a revocation sent afterwards is ineffective however quickly it arrives.
terms.find: Free at lom.agc.gov.my — Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136)

terms.gloss: Companies Act 2016 — personal liability for fraudulent trading.
terms.intermediate: Where the business has been carried on to defraud creditors, the court may declare that those knowingly party to it are personally liable for the company's debts.
terms.advanced: This is a statutory route past separate legal personality, and it needs actual dishonesty rather than mere insolvency or optimism. Fraud must be pleaded with particulars.
terms.find: Free at ssm.com.my and lom.agc.gov.my — Companies Act 2016 (Act 777)

terms.gloss: Penal Code s 6 — every offence is read with the General Exceptions.
terms.intermediate: Every definition of an offence in the Code is understood subject to the General Exceptions, even though the section defining the offence never mentions them.
terms.advanced: This is why a homicide answer that discusses only the Exceptions to s 300 has looked at half the picture. Sections 76 to 106 apply to every offence in the Code, and private defence lives there rather than in the offence sections. It is named in full here on purpose: the bare number is used in this app for more than one Act, so it is not auto-linked in prose. Look it up by name rather than expecting a hover.

terms.gloss: Restore the advantage received under a void agreement.
terms.intermediate: A person who has received any advantage under an agreement discovered to be void, or under a contract that becomes void, must restore it or make compensation.
terms.advanced: It does the work an English lawyer would look for in the law of restitution, and it is the provision to reach for when an answer has concluded that an agreement is void and stopped there. It applies both to agreements void from the outset and to contracts that become void, for example on frustration under s 57.

terms.gloss: The measure of damages for breach.
terms.intermediate: Compensation for loss arising naturally in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew when contracting to be likely to result. Remote and indirect loss is excluded.
terms.advanced: This is the rule in Hadley v Baxendale enacted, which changes how it is argued: the starting point is the section's words and the English cases illustrate how the two limbs have been applied. The explanation to s 74 requires the means available for remedying the inconvenience to be taken into account, which is the statutory foothold for mitigation.
terms.source: Contracts Act 1950 s 74; Hadley v Baxendale (1854) 9 Exch 341

terms.gloss: A sum named in the contract as payable on breach.
terms.intermediate: Reasonable compensation not exceeding the sum named, whether or not actual damage is proved to have been caused.
terms.advanced: The Malaysian position has moved. Selva Kumar required proof of actual loss and treated the named sum as a ceiling; Cubic Electronics reformulated the approach, drawing on Cavendish v Makdessi and directing attention to whether the clause protects a legitimate interest and whether the sum is out of all proportion to it. An answer giving only one of the two has not shown that it knows the position changed — and this is the most movable point in the contract module.
terms.source: Contracts Act 1950 s 75; Selva Kumar a/l Murugiah v Thiagarajah a/l Retnasamy [1995] 1 MLJ 817 (FC); Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd [2019] 2 MLJ 806 (FC)

terms.gloss: Penal Code s 99 — the outer limits of private defence.
terms.intermediate: Says when there is no right of private defence at all, and how far the right can ever go. If there was time to go to the authorities and no reasonable fear of death or grievous hurt, the right does not arise.
terms.advanced: Excess does not destroy a right that existed; it goes to whether the right extended this far. Answering those two questions in the wrong order is the commonest error in this area, and s 100 is where the right extends to causing death.

terms.gloss: Something a lender can fall back on if the borrower does not pay.
terms.intermediate: A charge over land and a guarantee from a third party are both security. They give the lender a second route to its money.
terms.advanced: Real security attaches to an asset and survives insolvency in a way personal security does not. That difference, not the paperwork, is why lenders want charges.

terms.gloss: An offence for which police may arrest without a warrant.
terms.intermediate: The Malaysian term for what English law calls an arrestable offence. Classification is done offence by offence in the First Schedule to the CPC.
terms.advanced: Using the English vocabulary signals that the answer is being written out of an English textbook, and the underlying scheme is not the same. A non-seizable offence generally requires a warrant or a summons, which changes the lawfulness of an arrest and therefore whether resisting it was an offence at all.

terms.gloss: The person who agrees to sell — the vendor.
terms.intermediate: A seller must deliver what was promised, with the right to sell it. A seller who has no title generally cannot give one.
terms.advanced: Nemo dat quod non habet is the default, and the exceptions are narrow and statutory. Under a Torrens register, registration itself can defeat the rule, which is why land is not analysed like goods.

terms.gloss: A company is a person in law, distinct from its members.
terms.intermediate: It owns its own property, makes its own contracts, sues and is sued in its own name, and its members are not liable for its obligations by reason only of membership.
terms.advanced: Everything else in company law follows from this: limited liability, the rule that a wrong to the company is the company's to complain of, and the concept of reflective loss. Salomon establishes that it holds even where one person owns and controls the whole company, and control alone is never a reason to disregard it.
terms.source: Companies Act 2016; Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22

terms.gloss: A subordinate court with a substantial civil limit and wide criminal jurisdiction.
terms.intermediate: Above the Magistrates' Court. It tries all offences except those punishable with death, and civil claims up to a statutory monetary limit.
terms.advanced: The monetary limits are statutory figures raised periodically, so they should be cited from a current source rather than remembered — a stale figure is the fastest way to be confidently wrong. On the criminal side the significant limit is the death penalty: a capital charge goes to the High Court.

terms.gloss: Of law: no longer in doubt. Of a case: ended by agreement rather than judgment.
terms.intermediate: Two different meanings share one word. Settled law is a position later courts treat as fixed; a settled case never reaches a decision at all.
terms.advanced: Settled law can still be departed from — the Federal Court is not absolutely bound by its own decisions. So *settled* is a description of practice, not a rule of law.

terms.gloss: A unit of ownership in a company.
terms.intermediate: A share is a bundle of rights against the company: to vote, to receive a dividend if one is declared, to a slice of what is left if it is wound up. It is not ownership of the company's assets.
terms.advanced: Because the shareholder owns the share and the company owns the assets, a fall in share value caused by a wrong to the company is reflective loss and not recoverable by the member.

terms.gloss: A person who owns shares in a company.
terms.intermediate: Someone who owns part of the company. They own shares — not the things the company owns — and they cannot hand the directors instructions.
terms.advanced: Also called a member. The distinction matters for who may sue: a wrong done to the company is the company's to complain of, and a fall in the value of every member's shares is reflective of that loss rather than a loss of their own.

terms.gloss: To put your name to a document, adopting it as yours.
terms.intermediate: A signature is evidence that you agreed to what the document says. Some transactions need one; many contracts need none at all.
terms.advanced: Section 340 turns on instruments that are forged or void, so proving whether a signature is genuine can decide who owns land. Handwriting is proved under section 45 or section 47 of the Evidence Act.

terms.gloss: Saying nothing — which the law sometimes reads and sometimes must not.
terms.intermediate: Silence is not acceptance in contract. In criminal procedure, an accused's silence is protected and generally cannot be held against them.
terms.advanced: Silence can become significant where there is a duty to speak — in a fiduciary relationship, or where a half-truth has been told, making non-disclosure a misrepresentation.

terms.gloss: Defamation in transient form.
terms.intermediate: Spoken defamation, generally actionable only on proof of special damage — with statutory exceptions that dispense with that requirement.
terms.advanced: The Defamation Act 1957 preserves and modifies the exceptions: words imputing unchastity or adultery to a woman or girl, and words calculated to disparage a person in an office, profession, calling, trade or business held at the time of publication, are actionable without special damage. Those categories carry the practical weight, because most slander claims fall inside one.

terms.gloss: Where a rule comes from, and therefore how strong it is.
terms.intermediate: Constitution, statute, case law, and in gaps English common law. A rule's source decides what can override it.
terms.advanced: Naming the source is the first move in any answer: it fixes the hierarchy, the method of interpretation and the ways the rule can be changed.

terms.gloss: Reviewing at growing intervals rather than in a block.
terms.intermediate: Distributing study over time so that each review happens as the memory begins to fade. This is what FSRS schedules for you.
terms.advanced: Intervals lengthen because each successful recall makes the trace more durable, so the optimal moment to test it again moves further out. Massed practice produces better performance during the session and worse retention after it, which is why a study method judged by how it feels will reliably pick the wrong one.

terms.gloss: An order compelling actual performance rather than damages.
terms.intermediate: A discretionary remedy governed by the Specific Relief Act 1950, not the Contracts Act. Section 11 sets out when it may be granted, s 20 when it may not.
terms.advanced: The gateway is the adequacy of damages, which is why it is a live remedy in a sale of land — each parcel being treated as unique — and rare for ordinary goods. Contracts requiring continuous supervision, and contracts for personal service, are outside it. Answering a specific performance question out of the Contracts Act is a category error.

terms.gloss: Spaced repetition system.
terms.intermediate: Software that schedules review at growing gaps, so you meet a card just as it starts to fade. This app uses one.
terms.advanced: An SRS trains recognition and recall of things you have already understood. It cannot teach reasoning, which is why the problem questions and the checkpoint blocks exist alongside it.

terms.gloss: Companies Commission of Malaysia.
terms.intermediate: The body you register a company with, and where company records are filed. Suruhanjaya Syarikat Malaysia is the Malay name the initials come from.
terms.advanced: Registration with SSM is the moment the company begins to exist as a separate person. Its filed records are also where a searcher establishes who the directors and shareholders actually are.

terms.gloss: Stand by what has been decided: a court is bound by the courts above it.
terms.intermediate: The doctrine that a court must follow the decisions of courts above it in the same hierarchy on the same point of law. It is what makes the law predictable enough to advise on.
terms.advanced: Three things have to line up before a decision binds: the same hierarchy, a superior court, and the same point of law. Malaysian courts sit in one hierarchy topped by the Federal Court, and decisions of foreign courts — including English ones — are never binding however eminent. The Federal Court may depart from its own previous decisions but does so sparingly and with reasons.

terms.gloss: A law made by a legislature.
terms.intermediate: An Act passed by Parliament or a State Legislature. A statute is the law itself; a case is evidence of what it means.
terms.advanced: Research runs in that order for a reason: find the Act, read the section, check it is the current reprint and that any amendment is in force, and only then look for cases. An answer that reasons from a case without naming the provision it construes has started in the middle.

terms.gloss: A member suing on the company's behalf, with leave.
terms.intermediate: Sections 347 to 350: a member, director or the Registrar may with leave of the court bring proceedings on behalf of the company to enforce the company's own right.
terms.advanced: Leave requires good faith and that the action is prima facie in the company's best interest, with notice to the company. It exists because a wrong to the company is the company's to complain of and the wrongdoers may control the board — the problem the old rule in Foss v Harbottle created and the statutory action solves.

terms.gloss: An offence needing no proof of a mental element.
terms.intermediate: Liability that attaches on proof of the prohibited act alone. It is the exception: the law presumes an offence requires a mental element unless the statute displaces it.
terms.advanced: The presumption is displaced expressly or by necessary implication, and courts look at the subject matter, the penalty, and whether requiring fault would frustrate the statute's purpose — regulatory offences with small penalties are the usual candidates. Even where the offence is strict, a defence of reasonable mistake of fact may survive, and the general exceptions in Chapter IV of the Penal Code continue to apply to offences under it.
terms.source: Standard presumption of construction; Penal Code s 6

terms.gloss: Removing a pleading that is bad as a document.
terms.intermediate: Order 18 rule 19: no reasonable cause of action or defence, scandalous or vexatious, prejudicial or embarrassing, or otherwise an abuse of process.
terms.advanced: On the first ground no evidence is admissible: the pleaded facts are assumed true and the question is whether they disclose a case. That is what separates it from summary judgment, which looks at the evidence. The jurisdiction is used sparingly and only in plain and obvious cases, and a difficult point of law is not by itself a reason to strike out.

terms.gloss: Governed by, or made to give way to.
terms.intermediate: *Subject to* sets a hierarchy: the provision that follows yields to the one named. Read the named provision first.
terms.advanced: *Notwithstanding* does the opposite, overriding what it names. Getting these two backwards inverts the meaning of a section, and it happens often.

terms.gloss: The Sessions and Magistrates' Courts.
terms.intermediate: The lower tier of the ordinary civil and criminal hierarchy, created by the Subordinate Courts Act 1948 rather than by the Courts of Judicature Act.
terms.advanced: The two statutes are the quickest way to keep the hierarchy straight: Courts of Judicature Act 1964 for the superior courts, Subordinate Courts Act 1948 for these. Their jurisdiction is entirely statutory, so a question about what one of them can do is always answered from the Act rather than from any inherent power.

terms.gloss: Law made under power delegated by an Act.
terms.intermediate: Rules, regulations, orders and by-laws made by a minister or other body under authority conferred by a parent Act. Valid only within the powers the parent confers.
terms.advanced: This is where the operative detail usually lives, and a research answer that reads the Act and stops has often missed the provision that decides the case. Its validity is always a question about the grant of power in the parent Act, which makes ultra vires the standard line of attack.

terms.gloss: What something really is, as against what it is called.
